POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:41:53 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.12 Dépendance aux Big Tech américaines : où en est la France par rapport à ses voisins européens ? https://www.politico.eu/article/ue-tech-americaine-dependance-souverainete-ia-cloud/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:41:42 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9396768 BRUXELLES — Même si l’UE est unie dans sa volonté de réduire sa dépendance aux technologies américaines, chaque Etat membre devra se débrancher de son côté — et certains auront bien plus d’efforts à fournir que d’autres.

Une étude menée par des chercheurs finlandais a mis en évidence de grandes disparités dans le degré de dépendance des Etats européens envers Amazon, Microsoft et Google pour les services publics numériques destinés aux citoyens.

“Cette variation n’est pas aléatoire, elle est systématique”, explique Vili Lehdonvirta, professeur de politique technologique à l’université finlandaise Aalto et coauteur du rapport.

Les chercheurs ont analysé les sites web gouvernementaux de 158 pays — notamment les portails permettant aux citoyens de trouver des informations, de déposer des demandes et d’effectuer des démarches administratives — afin d’évaluer dans quelle mesure ceux-ci dépendent des trois géants de la tech américaine.

Au sein de l’UE, Malte, la Finlande et l’Irlande affichent les parts les plus élevées de services publics nationaux hébergés par des hyperscalers américains : respectivement 78,5%, 56,1% et 45,8%.

En revanche, le taux estimé pour la France est de 9,3%, comparé à 2,9 % pour l’Allemagne.

La publication de cette étude intervient alors que l’UE négocie actuellement un projet de législation qui obligerait les administrations publiques à revoir leurs achats de solutions digitales américaines, dans un contexte marqué par les menaces répétées de Washington contre les politiques numériques de Bruxelles, de tentatives locales de se passer des services américains et les récentes pannes ayant affecté des outils informatiques très répandus.

Selon l’étude a révélé, Bahreïn présente le plus fort degré de dépendance au monde, les services américains hébergeant 81% des sites étudiés, tandis que la Russie et la Chine ne comptent aucun site public lié aux trois géants de la tech.

Les chercheurs ont constaté que les disparités dans le recours aux Big Tech tendent à être liées à la taille d’un pays et au coût du travail.

“L’explication est d’ordre économique : dans un grand pays, le marché domestique est mieux à même de soutenir des alternatives ou des technologies nationales, qui impliquent des investissements importants et des économies d’échelle élevées”, a détaillé Vili Lehdonvirta.

Pourquoi la taille compte

En Europe, la carte de la dépendance aux technologies américaines suit des tendances similaires, reflétant la taille du marché et le niveau de revenu. Cependant, elle est également plus contrastée en raison d’un ensemble hétéroclite de choix nationaux qui complique les efforts de l’UE visant à réduire ces dépendances stratégiques.

“Dans l’ensemble, on a cette configuration où les petits Etats membres ont recours au cloud américain et pas les grands Etats membres”, a décrit Vili Lehdonvirta. “Le cloud est un exemple de technologie qui nécessite un investissement initial important, et ensuite, plus on opère à grande échelle, plus elle est efficace.”

La méthodologie de l’étude présente certaines limites pour évaluer le degré de dépendance globale, car elle se concentre uniquement sur l’hébergement des services nationaux destinés au grand public, et non sur les systèmes locaux ni sur l’utilisation plus large de la technologie au sein de l’administration. Par exemple, Vili Lehdonvirta indique que les entités municipales — tels que les conseils d’école ou les systèmes de billetterie des piscines — sont plus susceptibles de recourir à des technologies américaines, la souveraineté numérique ne relevant pas de leurs compétences.

La taille et les revenus ne font pas tout non plus : les choix politiques déterminent également si les pays développent ou non des fournisseurs nationaux.

Au Royaume-Uni — la cinquième puissance mondiale —, 50,9% des sites gouvernementaux dépendent de technologies américaines, selon l’étude. Vili Lehdonvirta rappelle que l’exécutif britannique “a décidé, il y a environ quinze ans, de mettre le paquet sur le cloud dans le cadre d’une directive du gouvernement s’appliquant à tous les ministères et agences gouvernementales”. En l’absence d’alternatives nationales, “très rapidement, tout a migré vers le cloud américain. Aujourd’hui, il serait difficile de revenir en arrière, même s’ils le souhaitaient”, souligne-t-il.

De nouvelles règles à venir

La publication de cette étude intervient alors que les responsables politiques à Bruxelles débattent pour savoir où fixer les limites : les nouvelles règles proposées — dans le Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) — devraient-elles obliger les administrations publiques à réaliser des tests de souveraineté et à se tourner vers des alternatives européennes pour les secteurs les plus sensibles, ce qui pourrait évincer les géants américains de la tech ?

Rien que dans le secteur privé, les entreprises européennes dépensent environ 330 milliards d’euros par an en services cloud et logiciels américains, ce qui confère à la tech américaine une part de marché estimée à 83% selon une étude de 2025.

Mais les Etats membres n’ont pas tous intérêt à des règles strictes en la matière. Cela dépend en partie s’ils ont ou non des fournisseurs nationaux prêts à rivaliser.

Josh Kallmer, directeur des affaires internationales chez Zoom, dont le siège est aux Etats-Unis, estime pour sa part qu’une approche de niveau européen permettrait d’éviter une fragmentation. “Cette fragmentation supplémentaire affecte une entreprise comme la nôtre”, a-t-il déclaré lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO. “Chaque restriction supplémentaire mise en place a un impact beaucoup plus important sur la liberté de choix dans les pays de taille moyenne et les petits pays.”

Les négociateurs du CADA en sont pleinement conscients. “Nous devons essayer de mettre en place un cadre clair afin que les 27 pays aient la même interprétation de la loi, car, en fin de compte, le but est de faciliter la tâche des PME en Europe”, dit Diego Solier, eurodéputé membre des Conservateurs et réformistes européens, qui est l’un des principaux négociateurs sur ce dossier.

Pour le coauteur de l’étude, Vili Lehdonvirta, ce texte risque de rater sa cible s’il ne répartit pas plus équitablement les coûts et avantages au sein de l’UE.

“Le coût de la mise en conformité de cette politique pèse principalement sur les petits Etats membres, tandis que ses avantages, à savoir l’augmentation de l’activité économique, profitent surtout aux grands Etats membres”, développe-t-il. “Si nous ne disposons d’aucun mécanisme de partage des charges, le résultat final sera similaire à ce que nous observons actuellement, c’est-à-dire une sorte de tentative timide qui n’oblige pas vraiment qui que ce soit à agir.”

]]> en Bank of England boss warns AI must benefit humans https://www.politico.eu/article/bank-of-england-boss-warns-ai-must-benefit-humans/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9397860 LONDON — Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned governments need to reassure the public about the benefits of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models, amid rising fears the technology is advancing at a pace beyond human control.

As the U.K. prepares to take over the G20 presidency, Bailey backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s plan to put AI at the heart of the country’s plans.

But the U.K. central banker said lawmakers, not regulators, would have to set the guardrails for the technology.

“It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were,” he said in an interview from his office in the Bank of England.

With the G20 presidency fast approaching, Burnham has said he wants to use the U.K. to establish “a single set” of global standards for AI.

U.S. President Donald Trump shot down any global oversight of the giant American companies dominating the development of the technology, which he has rebranded as “super intelligence.”

Against that backdrop, Bailey called for more international testing and access to AI giants’ frontier models, which he said are “critical questions” as the U.K. takes on the G20 presidency.

The U.K. central banking chief will make that push internationally in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog for the financial system.

With the number of cyber incidents already rising, Bailey said AI models are being built on “the good, the bad, and the ugly” of human behavior, and are now training themselves.

But the governor argued it was reasonable for the public to ask what the benefit is from the rapid growth of a technology which could be used to blow holes in the financial system, but also order the Christmas shopping.

“The public needs to trust this technology,” he said. “There needs to be greater transparency, explanation of what the things do, how they do it, what we’re doing.”

He added: “It’s sensible to come at it from that angle and say, we’ve got to have stronger government understanding, stronger government coordination on this stuff. Regulation may follow it.”

The U.K. central banker is acutely aware of the threats the new technology could bring to the financial system. The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee report on Thursday spelled out risks including increasingly interconnected and opaque financing that could spread the pain should a potential stock market AI bubble burst.

But Bailey said he would put himself in a camp of people who want AI to succeed to improve productivity and well-being.

“But it has to be under human control,” he said. “We want AI to be used by humans, as it were.”

]]> en Ukraine cajoles allies to keep Putin’s athletes out https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-pushes-allies-keep-russian-athletes-out-putin-international-sport-restrictions/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9381537 BRUSSELS — Kyiv is stepping up its bid to keep Russian athletes out of global sports tournaments.

“We cannot allow international sport to become the weak link in the democratic world,” Ukrainian Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi told POLITICO from Brussels, where he met EU sports ministers, as legal and political momentum builds for Russian competitors to return.

International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry has said athletes should not pay for governmental actions; top sporting organizations have eased restrictions instituted in 2022 after the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion began; and a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling overturned ice hockey’s ban on Russian teams.

Ukraine has near-unanimous EU backing for keeping Russian athletes out of European sport, and wants the bloc’s new visa ban on Moscow’s combatants also applied to soldiers who compete on national teams, Bidnyi added.

With the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics on the horizon, the dispute is becoming a test of who’ll shape Russia’s return to world sport: governments, or federations and courts. Kyiv is desperate for Europe to coordinate its response before more restrictions are lifted.

Bidnyi said he presented three demands to EU sports ministers on Nov. 20: a ban on Russian symbols; verified neutral status for athletes; and funding cuts for federations that let Russians compete. He added that the proposals found “wide support.”

“I have heard no voice against it,” Bidnyi said. Asked whether all 27 EU countries are on board, he said that “almost all of them” had expressed willingness to make it a common position.

No propaganda in sport

On Monday, the European Commission proposed barring Russian teams and athletes from competing in the EU, which would also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European sports and cultural associations. The sanctions package needs the approval of all 27 member countries.

In addition, seven EU countries had written to European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before the sanctions package was presented asking for tougher visa rules on Russian nationals.

The countries wanted the Commission’s guidelines on visa applications by Russians to prevent nonessential travel, including to sporting events, rather than wait for a revised Visa Code that is not expected before the first quarter of 2027. They also encouraged fellow EU countries not to grant visas to Russian or Belarusian athletes.

Bidnyi said his three points are designed to stop Russia from using sport for propaganda, while Moscow maintains a relentless bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.

The first measure is a ban on Russian symbols, such as flags or the national anthem. “It’s unacceptable that the anthem of a country that kills peaceful people in Europe today sounds in such a cheerful manner in European arenas,” he said.

The second is to make “neutral athlete” status something that is actually verified. “The neutral status should be maintained by detailed checking,” Bidnyi said. “We must check all aspects.”

The third is money. Bidnyi pointed to the new EU restriction on Erasmus+ funding — the bloc’s main program for education, training, youth and sport — for organizations that allow Russian state symbols, calling it a “first concrete result.” He wants the same model widened to organizations that let Russians use sport as a “tool of propaganda,” whether or not symbols are involved.

Bidnyi also raised the issue of soldiers that have become athletes, which touches the EU’s newest migration measures. The Commission’s visa guidelines, published this week alongside the sanctions package, tell national authorities to refuse visas to anyone who has served in Russia’s armed forces and fought in the war.

Bidnyi said the International Paralympic Committee has tolerated combatants taking part in its events, and that Russia is now trying to put soldiers who fought in Ukraine on its Paralympic teams. He called that “absolutely unacceptable.” Europe, he said, already refuses visas to combatants, and “it should be like this.”

The IPC said it has no rules barring former soldiers from competing, pointing to the movement’s origins in rehabilitating injured war veterans after World War II.

Nor is it its role, the IPC added, “to make moral judgments on which injured soldiers should or should not be allowed to compete.” It said former soldiers from countries including the U.S., Britain, Iraq, Bosnia and Iran have competed, and that it expects more at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The IPC said its responsibility is to decide which national Paralympic committees and athletes are eligible and to enforce its conduct rules. It said accreditation for the Games is the final decision of the organizing committee and national authorities, which handle security and background checks. Their organization’s answer did not mention Russia or Ukraine.

Russia’s sports minister, who the EU has also sanctioned, stated in September that more than 70 war veterans were already on national teams. Bidnyi also alleged that the Russian Union of Martial Arts recruits on behalf of units fighting in Ukraine and trains drone operators, and said that should be prohibited.

The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Bidnyi’s assertions about Russia’s military recruitment and wider propaganda strategy.

Ice hockey backlash

Sporting institutions, however, are gradually moving toward Russian reinstatement.

On one side of the confrontation, Bidnyi said, are governing bodies, courts and federations, which are “gradually opening the door to Russians hiding behind claims of neutrality.”

His primary example is the Oct. 30 decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn the International Ice Hockey Federation’s ban on Russian teams for the 2026-27 season. “The hockey case is the most outrageous example of Russian influence,” Bidnyi said.

Asked for comment, CAS said that the case, brought by the Russian Ice Hockey Federation against the IIHF, “was decided on a strictly legal basis” and that it is not aware of any circumstance that could have affected the panel’s independence.

Ultimately, that ruling set off a backlash. Finland, Sweden, Czechia, Norway, Austria, Denmark and Latvia have said they will play at next May’s men’s world championship in Germany but not against Russia — which means almost half of the 16 teams are refusing to face Russia. Canada’s government said Russia will not be allowed to play at the world juniors there next month.

Sponsors are also balking, with Skoda, the tournament’s main sponsor, saying it will reassess its backing. The IIHF says it still disagrees with the ruling.

Sanctions have also been lifted in gymnastics, weightlifting and chess, and the international ski federation has cleared more than 400 Russian and Belarusian athletes and support staff to compete as neutrals this season.

Bidnyi expects more of the same. The IOC’s decision to reinstate the Russian Olympic Committee, he said, “has set a dangerous precedent. International federations may now begin lifting restrictions one after another, hiding behind the autonomy of sport.”

Moscow, Bidnyi said, will keep going back to CAS and present every readmission as a propaganda win, with Putin personally overseeing the effort.

On the other side, he said, are governments, which can take a “principled stand” and refuse to let Russian representatives or the symbols of an aggressor state onto their territory. Russian participation “has long ceased to be merely a matter of sporting regulations,” he said. “It is a question of national security.”

The next chance to build a common position is a meeting of sports ministers in Tallinn in January. Bidnyi said it could bring in non-EU countries such as Canada and Norway, which have already taken firm action.

]]> en Spain’s looming right-wing pivot on climate is already playing out in Valencia https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-looming-right-wing-pivot-on-climate-is-already-playing-out-in-valencia/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9363876 VALENCIA — Spain’s climate agenda could be in for a radical shake-up if conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo takes power alongside the far-right Vox party after Sunday’s election — a prospect already playing out in Valencia.

Feijóo has pledged to scrap what he calls “unrealistic” timelines for climate goals, arguing that Spain must pursue decarbonization at a more pragmatic pace. His center-right People’s Party argues that climate ambitions must not come at the expense of economic competitiveness, industry or households.

His likely coalition partners, the far-right Vox party, want to go further — promising to dismantle what they call “climate impositions” from Brussels, remove low-emission zones and reverse restrictions on combustion-engine cars and CO₂ emissions.

The two parties’ dismantling of climate policy can already be seen in Spain’s Valencia region, where the PP has governed with Vox’s backing since 2023, coinciding with a rollback of environmental protections and the deadly floods of October 2024.

“The dangerous climate skepticism that will define a PP-Vox government at the national level has been on display here in Valencia from the moment they took power,” warned Raül Camacho Segarra, a spokesperson for the Valencian grassroots movement working to rebuild flood-damaged areas responsibly.

The floods put the government’s approach to land use, environmental regulation and climate adaptation under intense scrutiny. Yet shortly after, PP politician Juanfran Pérez Llorca was sworn in as the region’s new president and reaffirmed his opposition to parts of the climate agenda, describing the center-right European People’s Party’s Green Deal as a “threat” to Valencia’s farmers.

Local critics like Camacho accuse the right-wing government of failing to learn the lessons of the disaster and endangering the region’s communities.

“The policies they instituted ahead of the floods made us more vulnerable, and instead of recalibrating after the tragedy, they’ve actually doubled down since 2024,” he said, pointing to the allocation of public funds to bullfighting events instead of emergency response and promoting construction in areas needed for flood prevention.

Ana Camarasa, a physical geographer and regional flood risk expert at the University of Valencia, questioned politicians’ ability to pursue effective long-term resilience strategies while casting doubt on the threat posed by climate change.

“Governments that deny climate change ultimately aren’t obliged to take measures to address it, because it’s a problem that officially doesn’t exist,” she said.

Controversial climate record

With its millions of voters, Spain’s fourth-most-populous region is a coveted prize in the country’s political battle for power.

After eight years of left-wing rule, in 2023 the PP teamed up with Vox to take control of Valencia, forming one of its first regional coalition governments with the far right.

Under regional president Carlos Mazón, the new administration moved to scrap plans for a regional emergency response unit, dismantled key elements of Valencia’s climate law and emissions taxes, and disbanded a newly created agency to monitor climate change. His government also eased rules governing development on flood-prone coastlines and protected agricultural land.

Those decisions came under renewed scrutiny on Oct. 29, 2024, when Valencia was hit by one of the deadliest floods in modern Spanish history. The regional government downplayed the threat posed by a powerful storm that swept through the region, unleashing torrential rain that inundated towns and killed 229 people.

For months after the disaster, Mazón — who controversially remained at an hours-long private lunch as the floodwaters rose — refused to take responsibility for his government’s handling of the catastrophe. Although crisis management is a regional responsibility, the PP shifted blame onto the national government and then-Deputy Prime Minister Teresa Ribera.

But Spanish courts exonerated both national authorities and Ribera, noting the regional government was the only entity authorized to manage the crisis. After being denounced as an “assassin” by victims’ relatives one year on, Mazón finally stepped down.

His successor, Pérez Llorca, took office promising to rebuild the region and leave it better prepared for future disasters. Yet key climate-protection measures have been further weakened since the floods.

Weeks after the disaster, the government pressed ahead with legislative changes to allow construction closer to shorelines. More recently, other controversial proposals have surfaced, including a plan to build more than 1,200 homes on farmland that critics say is instrumental to absorbing water during torrential rainstorms.

In an interview, Raúl Mérida, the technocrat appointed to oversee the region’s recovery, defended its reconstruction and adaptation efforts while playing down the significance of the Valencian government’s climate-skeptic statements.

“Our actions are based on science,” he said, adding that politicians across the political spectrum had backed his proposals to build floodable parks and carry out environmentally conscious river-restoration schemes that aim to better protect communities against future storms.

According to Mérida, 98% of infrastructure damaged in the disaster has been rebuilt. But he acknowledged that rebuilding did not necessarily mean the region was now better protected against flooding.

“The emergency contracts only allowed us to restore the infrastructure that was there, not improve it,” he said, citing roads and bridges. “We had to rebuild some infrastructure that had proved inadequate in reducing the severity of the floods in the same way.”

He added that the government had reinforced foundations and added protective stone embankments. When it came to private homes, he said, things were more complicated: Residents often had deep family roots and longstanding ties to the communities where they lived.

Like other rapidly growing Spanish regions, Mérida said Valencia was under pressure to build more housing and had enough land to do so as long as flood-zone regulations were respected. But he insisted that the priority would be ensuring “regulations governing flood-prone areas are respected” and that “citizens and territory are protected.”

“Adaptation measures work just as well in a left-wing municipality as they do in a right-wing one,” he said, adding that protecting communities from extreme weather should transcend party lines.

The limits of green consensus

In a September POLITICO poll carried out by PF Global, 60% of Spanish respondents described climate change as either the most important or one of the most important issues of our time.

But the poll also suggests Spaniards are wary of climate action overshadowing other national priorities. Nearly half — 49.2% — said the country’s energy and environmental policies were diverting resources from other pressing issues, including the cost-of-living crisis, healthcare and housing. Just over half — 50.3% — said Spain should act on climate change but not more than other countries.

That national ambivalence could give the PP and Vox room to argue for a slower, less costly green transition — even as voters continue to regard climate change as a major concern.

Widespread anger over the deadly 2024 floods doesn’t seem to have weakened the right-wing bloc’s electoral prospects in the region: A range of polls project the PP and Vox could win 19 of the region’s 33 seats in Spain’s 350-seat parliament.

In Valencia’s central province (excluding Castellón and Alicante), where 16 seats are up for grabs, Vox is projected to double its representation, from two seats in 2023 to four in 2026.

David Ribó, a candidate for the left-wing regionalist Compromís-Front Valencià coalition, said he was dismayed by the polling: “It boggles the mind that in a region that is the epicenter of climate change, political options that are openly denialist are still attracting votes.”

Ribó argued that Vox’s success did not reflect public apathy to climate change, but rather frustration with mainstream parties, as seen in the immediate aftermath of the floods, when the populist slogan “sólo el pueblo salva el pueblo” (“only the people can save the people”) was directed at political leaders and institutions perceived to have abandoned the region.

“People are struggling to make ends meet — especially because of the insane prices they’re having to pay for housing — and naturally, there is a sense of discontent,” he said. The “inequality crisis,” he argued, is pushing disillusioned voters toward populist leaders.

The University of Valencia’s Camarasa expressed concern over the increasing climate skepticism in Spanish politics, arguing certain topics “shouldn’t be treated as an ideological matter: The data is there, and we’ve also seen the consequences that come when you ignore it.”

The issue, she added, was particularly relevant amid the country’s housing crisis, which has put politicians under pressure to fast-track construction. Pointing to the deadly consequences of homes being built in flood-prone areas, she warned that leaders’ dismissive attitude toward the climate threat could lead to further “deficient and ineffective land management.”

But she conceded that Spain’s political system was perhaps not built to address the threat the country faces. “A government lasts as long as it lasts, but the solutions have to last longer,” she said.

]]> en Swingin’ on the flippity-flop with chicken nuggets: The perils of young people’s slang https://www.politico.eu/article/swingin-on-the-flippity-flop-with-chicken-nuggets-the-perils-of-young-peoples-slang/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9395943 Welcome to Declassified, a weekly humor column.

In August 1992, this writer put on his wack slack, fuzz and kickers before swingin’ on the flippity-flop watching popular rock combo Nirvana in a muddy field in southern England.

Fear not, the water at POLITICO Towers hasn’t been laced with ketamine. I’m just reliving a journalistic nightmare: young people and their new words.

Three months after I stood in a field listening to “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” a journalist from The New York Times called up Sub Pop, the record label that released Nirvana’s first album and did more than any other to give the world grunge, and fell victim to a prank.

Megan Jasper, a one-time receptionist at the label who went on to become its CEO, proceeded to make up a list of fake slang terms being used by the kids of the day. The NYT published the list in full*.

When it comes to politics, it’s hard to know what’s worse: pretending to be down with the kids when you’re old enough to know better or being clearly out-of-touch and missing out on what the youth really care about.

This week, Andy “have I mentioned I like The Smiths” Burnham was stung after getting too close to the TikTok generation (a bit like Icarus flying too close to the sun, if Icarus was the British prime minister and the sun was people doing shitty dances).

Burnham invited a bunch of creators to an event earlier this month (what’s the collective noun for influencers? A virus?) but footage only emerged this week of one miming the words “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets” outside the famous black door of No. 10 Downing Street.

Bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets is a) an unwieldy name for a pet, b) a good name for a punk band, and c) offensive if you understand what young people are talking about (‘bomboclaat’ is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, ‘pussy’ is a slang term for female genitals, and some accounts reckon ‘chicken nuggets’ refers to women being ‘cheap white meat’ — although it could also just mean chicken assholes and eyelashes mashed up, breadcrumbed and deep-fried).

Social media influencer Max Balegde, who posted the offending video, has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram. To put that into perspective, this column sometimes reaches the dizzying heights of eight readers.

The EU is so desperately uncool that no one has ever shouted “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets” outside the Berlaymont. Despite a campaign to get countries to put forward the names of influencers to attend European Councils, a grand total of zero turned up at the October summit because of an overwhelming lack of interest from all sides.

* Wack slack = old ripped jeans

* Fuzz = heavy wool sweater

* Kickers = boots

* Swingin’ on the flippity-flop = hangin’ out

]]> en Spain’s right turn: What a PP-Vox government would mean for Madrid — and Brussels https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-right-turn-what-pp-vox-government-would-mean-for-madrid-brussels/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9384954 MADRID — After eight years of Socialist rule, polls point to an incoming right-wing government in Spain — but exactly what it’ll do in office will depend on the balance of power between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox.

The right-wing parties’ manifestos are light on specifics. In the PP’s case, that is a deliberate strategy, according to one official, so that party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo can avoid overpromising in the campaign.

The exact agenda would depend on how ministries are carved up in a coalition between Feijóo’s traditional center-right party and Santiago Abascal’s Vox, which is still weighing how involved it wants to be in a potential Feijóo administration.

But a rightward shift after eight years of Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist government would shake up Spain’s policy agenda in several key areas, from migration to data centers, and certainly draw attention in Brussels.

One thing is clear, though: Spain is unlikely to turn into a euroskeptic at the top EU table.

Vox may be fiercely critical of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and the EU institutions, but it knows there are limits to how far you can press euroskepticism in Spain. The country is, at heart, very pro-European: Its path to EU membership ran alongside its transition to democracy after the death of fascist leader General Francisco Franco, and Europe is part of the country’s democratic identity.

Here are six ways Spain’s policy agenda could change under the PP-Vox government.

Migration: Spaniards first?

Migration is one area where Sánchez-era policy is likely to be reversed.

Both PP and Vox have strongly criticized the current government’s mass regularization of migrants, and the PP also advocates for a legal ban on this type of measure.

Since the last election in 2023, migration has risen to second on Spaniards’ list of top concerns, behind housing. The Ceuta crisis — where tens of thousands of mainly young men from Morocco poured into Spain — has hardened the rhetoric of both Vox and the PP, which have embraced the term “invasion.”

Vox’s flagship policy on migration is known as “national priority,” essentially a Spaniards-first approach that gives preferential access to public services, from housing to schools and benefits. Feijóo’s party manifesto includes “priority criteria for access to certain benefits, services and public resources,” but the PP doesn’t limit the criteria to nationality, saying it should also cover long-term legal residents in Spain.

Vox has also made remigration — a term imported from far-right circles in Germany and Austria — one of its core election campaign proposals. But the European Commission has already found that remigration proposals cannot be squared with EU law and the PP distances itself from the idea.

On almost all other migration-related issues, the PP and Vox would align with the new mainstream in an EU that takes a much tougher line, including the idea of return hubs.

Agriculture: Vox’s turf

The far right frames rural Spain as the true heart of the nation. Abascal’s party has always tried to secure the agriculture departments in regional governments where it rules jointly with the PP — and the agriculture ministry would likely be one of its top targets in a coalition government.

A significant proportion of immigration in Spain is linked to the agricultural sector, which relies on a vast pool of cheap migrant labor. Vox has spoken of extending the national priority principle to this sector as well, calling for pay rises to make these jobs attractive to Spaniards, although it has avoided making it a central issue of its immigration policy. The PP proposes temporary visas and hiring in the workers’ home countries.

Spain could end up clashing with the EU over trade if a PP-Vox government seeks to restrict imports from countries it thinks undercut the local market. In the past, Abascal’s party has also sought the suspension of a farm goods deal with Morocco, arguing that Moroccan producers were creating “unfair competition.” The PP pledges that “imported foodstuffs will meet food safety and production standards equivalent to our own,” a call for so-called mirror clauses in trade deals.

Vox rejects the EU Mercosur trade deal with South America as an attack on Spanish producers, while the PP tries to avoid the Mercosur debate, but is generally in favor of the pact.

However, the PP and Vox are completely aligned with the current Socialist government in their rejection of cuts to the Common Agricultural Policy — the EU’s all-important subsidy scheme for farmers — in the next 7-year EU budget, so there will be continuity on that.

Tech: no more crusades against Big Tech

Sánchez has made his testy relationship with what he calls the “technoligarchs” an important part of his election message. That public crusade against Big Tech will disappear with a PP-Vox government. Abascal has met Elon Musk, who has publicly supported Vox.

But on some issues, the PP is not far from the Socialist Party. For example, Feijóo pledges to bar social media access to those under 14 and accuses Sánchez’s government of being too soft on child protection on social media. On the other hand, Vox opposes this type of age limit.

Data centers could prove a bigger change. A Socialist decree that establishes limits on data centers’ energy consumption and sovereignty conditions was just approved by the government and ratified by parliament. Alberto Nadal, Feijóo’s industry guru, has promised to repeal this law once in government, clearing the way for potential sectoral expansion.

Energy and climate: from vanguard to mainstream

Energy and climate change have been major political priorities of the Socialist government, putting Spain among the most ambitious countries in the EU on green issues. Expect that to change substantially under a PP-Vox government.

Just by how much will depend on support for Vox. Abascal’s party links many of Spain’s agricultural problems to climate rules and has been mobilizing its supporters against the climate agenda for years. Vox has, for example, criticized the uprooting of olive trees to make way for solar panels.

The PP is firmly in the new EU mainstream on climate and energy, aligning with the European People’s Party to advocate a relaxation of climate rules and “an end to the imposition of unrealistic timelines.”

On the energy front, both parties agree on extending the lifespan of nuclear plants. But even if Vox tries to pull Spain away from the energy transition, renewable energy is already a reality: Renewable electricity increased from 35% of total generation in 2015 to 56% in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency.

China: harder stance?

Under Sánchez’s government, Spain became one of the EU’s biggest advocates for closer ties with Beijing and established a strategic dialogue with China’s Xi Jinping.

Feijóo has promised he would abide by any EU-level agreement to harden the bloc’s stance towards Beijing. And some of Feijóo’s closest aides on foreign policy, such as veteran diplomat Ildefonso Castro, are committed Atlanticists who could steer a PP prime minister toward a tougher position if that aligned with Washington.

Vox is hawkish on China and in 2025 accused Sánchez of flattering “the communist Chinese dictatorship.” Both parties on the right support excluding high-risk suppliers from public procurement, citing Huawei as an example, and have strongly criticized the current government’s renewal of contracts with the Chinese company.

But it’s not an easy call. Some of the biggest Chinese investments in Spain are in regions with PP-led governments, such as Galicia, Andalusia and Valencia.

Women’s rights and culture wars

Sánchez’s government has sought to champion progressive values on the international stage, and a Spanish government with Vox as junior partner would mark a sharp contrast with that.

During his campaign, Feijóo promised to strip the ministry of equality of its ministerial status and incorporate its responsibilities, which are mainly focused on gender, into another department. If Vox’s model for regional governments is followed, Abascal’s party will seek to establish a family ministry.

In a radio interview, Feijóo also opened a debate on a possible reform of Spain’s abortion law, arguing that the parents of minors who decide to have an abortion should be informed of this decision. Vox, which in 2023 advocated repealing the law, is now more vague.

But there are points of friction between the two parties on equality. The PP maintains the consensus on gender violence laws, while Vox usually talks about intrafamilial violence and calls for the repeal of laws that have criminalized men.

Equality aside, expect to see culture war battles over rural heritage come into government. Vox supports measures to protect hunting, and both the PP and Vox agree on hunting wolves to protect livestock in the north of the country.

But the biggest battleground has been over bullfighting. Current Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun, from the left-wing Sumar party, scrapped the national bullfighting prize in 2024. Both PP and Vox plan to reinstate it.

Both the conservative People's Party, the PP, and the far-right Vox have seized on Spain's relationship with Rabat to attack the current socialist government.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

As Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday, one issue has been gaining prominence in the campaign: Morocco. Both the conservative People’s Party, the PP, and the far-right Vox have seized on Spain’s relationship with Rabat to attack the current socialist government.

So, why has Morocco become a political flashpoint, and what are the candidates positions?

Pedro Sánchez’s opponents have found a way to challenge him: they accuse him of being too soft on Morocco. They point to the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta in July, accusing Morocco of allowing thousands of people to cross into the Spanish enclave as a way of putting pressure on Madrid.

But tensions between the two countries go much further than migration.

For decades, Spain and Morocco have also been at odds over Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony. Morocco considers the territory part of its own country, while the Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, seeks independence for the Sahrawi people.

Read more

Sanchez’s snap election, and what his defeat would mean for Spain’s Nato spending

The dispute remains unresolved. A UN-backed referendum on self-determination has never taken place. There used to be a UN peacekeeping mission in the territory, but it ended earlier this month after its mandate was not renewed.

Now, what role did Pedro Sanchez play in all of that? In 2022, he made a major diplomatic shift by backing Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara. 

Under the proposal, Western Sahara would have its own institutions and manage its internal affairs, but remain under Moroccan sovereignty, rather than becoming an independent state.

The move helped bring an end to a diplomatic crisis between Madrid and Rabat and opened a new chapter in their relationship. But this summer’s mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta has put that relationship under renewed scrutiny.

The question is whether Morocco deliberately allowed people to cross into the Spanish enclave to put pressure on Madrid. And Spanish authorities themselves have reached different conclusions.

The National Intelligence Centre, Spain’s intelligence agency, found no evidence that the Moroccan state organised the influx. And that’s essentially the basis for Sánchez’s position.

However, a report by the National Police’s immigration and border centre, published in September, painted a different picture. It described what investigators saw as a coordinated movement and alleged that Moroccan security forces had actively facilitated some crossings.

The report did not establish that the Moroccan government had ordered or organised the influx. But the issue has become a political weapon in Spain’s election campaign.

So what are the candidates’s position? Vox leader Santiago Abascal has described the events in Ceuta as a hybrid war waged by Morocco. For him, normal relations with Rabat are simply impossible under the current circumstances.

Read more

Lula’s online ‘army’ shows how copying Brazil’s WhatsApp model could backfire on Spain and France’s left

Vox is calling for the suspension of international agreements and a review of diplomatic relations with Morocco until the country respects what the party calls Spain’s borders and sovereignty in Ceuta and Melilla, its other North African enclave.

The conservative PP is also taking a tougher stance. Its leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, has described the mass crossings as an invasion and an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity.

Feijóo says he wants to reset the relationship and rebalance Spain’s ties with both Rabat and Algiers. That matters because Algeria and Morocco have very different positions on Western Sahara, and Spain’s diplomatic shift in favour of Morocco’s autonomy plan has strained its relations with Algeria.

That’s why Morocco is watching the elections closely. According to Yabiladi, a news outlet focused on Morocco and its diaspora, the dispute with Morocco gives the PP and Vox an opportunity to mobilise voters around sensitive issues such as territorial sovereignty, immigration, security and national identity.

But a change of government might not necessarily mean a complete overhaul of Spain’s relationship with Morocco.

Although the PP has criticised Sánchez’s approach, Feijóo has so far offered relatively few details on what a new relationship with Morocco would look like in practice.

For now, the PP is leading in the polls, roughly three points ahead of Sánchez’s socialist party, while Vox is in third place, according to the latest polling averages.

Most polls suggest that a coalition between the PP and Vox could secure a majority in parliament.

But the race is still relatively close, and much will depend on the final results and the negotiations that follow.

]]> Czech PM Babiš courts missile defences after secret talks with Israeli intelligence chiefs https://euobserver.com/251941/czech-pm-babis-courts-missile-defences-after-secret-talks-with-israeli-intelligence-chiefs/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:37:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251941 The Czech prime minister met Israeli intelligence chiefs and held talks with arms manufacturers about buying anti-missile defence on his most recent trip to Jerusalem. ]]> First published in Deník N.

Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš met Israeli intelligence chiefs during his recent three-day trip to Israel, which also saw him explore the purchase of anti-missile defence systems.

Alongside Miroslav Toman, head of the Czech foreign intelligence service (ÚZSI), the Czech premier met Roman Gofman, the new chief of Mossad, the Israeli foreign intelligence service, and his deputies. Gofman, who took the Mossad leadership position in June, previously served as military secretary to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

It follows a similar visit in April, when Czech foreign minister Petr Macinka and former ÚZSI chief Vladimír Posoldaalso also met Mossad’s leadership.

Read more

Fastest EU citizens’ initiative ever pushes Brussels to end EU‑Israel trade agreement

    ]]>         Lula’s online ‘army’ shows how copying Brazil’s WhatsApp model could backfire on Spain and France’s left https://euobserver.com/251777/lulas-online-army-shows-how-copying-brazils-whatsapp-model-could-backfire-on-spains-and-frances-left/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:00:49 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251777 With Spain voting on Sunday and France preparing for its 2027 presidential election, the Brazilian 'digital army' experiment appears to offer an appealing solution to the far-right's dominance of online political communication. But there is a problem: barely a month after Lula's victory, his online army has found a new enemy and it’s not the far-right, but the Left itself.]]> Europe’s Left believes it may have found a formula for defeating the far-right.

    Following Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election last month, progressive movements in France and Spain began replicating the digital mobilisation strategy developed by congressman André Janones, whose WhatsApp channel, Exército do Lula (Lula’s Army), attracted nearly 11 million followers.

    With Spain voting on Sunday (29 November) and France preparing for its 2027 presidential election, the Brazilian experiment appears to offer an appealing solution to the far-right’s dominance of online political communication. 

    But there is a problem: barely a month after Lula’s victory, his digital army has found a new enemy and it’s not the far-right, but the Left itself.

    The channel that once mobilised millions against Bolsonaro is now being used to attack leftwing politicians and activists who oppose the government’s proposed fiscal adjustment – that was swiftly approved with the full support of the far-right.

    Read more

    Trump cheers Bolsonaro Jr’s advance on Lula in Brazil, but EU fears for Mercosur alliance

    Among its targets are members of the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), that supported the re-election of Lula da Silva, critics concerned about the potential consequences of fiscal restraint for public services and the poor, and even politicians of the president’s own Workers’ Party (PT).

    Janones has accused sections of the left of sabotaging Lula’s government, while more than 1.4 million followers have reportedly abandoned his channel since the election.

    The irony is difficult to ignore as a digital instrument celebrated for defending democracy against authoritarianism and the dangers of a new far-right government is now being deployed to discourage legitimate democratic disagreement.

    Lessons for Europe

    And this is precisely what European progressives should be examining before rushing to import Janones’ methods.

    There is no denying the effectiveness of his electoral strategy since through carefully coordinated messaging, viral content and instructions to millions of followers, Janones helped challenge Flavio Bolsonaro’s formidable digital machinery.

    Yet the electoral success of this operation should not obscure its fundamental limitations: mobilising millions of people to distribute political messages is not the same as empowering them to participate in political decisions.

    What happens when the candidate wins? Are those supporters expected to continue following orders, defending every government decision, regardless of their political convictions?

    That appears to be the contradiction confronting Lula’s Army.

    Its followers were instrumentalised as political combatants, receiving instructions about what to share, amplify and attack but they were never part of a democratic organisation capable of collectively deciding its political direction.

    When supporters began expressing dissatisfaction with Lula’s fiscal proposals, many responded to messages with scissors emojis, symbolising their opposition to potential spending cuts. Rather than engaging with their objections, Janones turned against critics within the left.

    It is an especially troubling development considering the historical relationship between Lula’s Workers’ Party and competing leftwing movements.

    In 2003, the PT expelled parliamentarians who opposed Lula’s pension reform, helping precipitate the creation of PSOL. During Brazil’s mass demonstrations in June 2013, the party struggled to understand the mobilisation and mostly backed the repression that followed.

    In the next few years, every possible leadership inside and outside the party was neutralised and coopted, and even PSOL ended up becoming nothing more than an appendage of Lula’s party. 

    Limitations of relying on WhatsApp

    The Brazilian experience also raises uncomfortable questions about the growing dependence of progressive politics on personalised leadership and privately controlled digital platforms as WhatsApp channels can disseminate information with extraordinary efficiency, but they cannot, by themselves, replace trade unions, grassroots organisations, political assemblies or the slower, often frustrating process of democratic deliberation.

    A movement of millions that cannot meaningfully question its leadership may be an impressive electoral machine, but it is hardly a democratic revolution, and this is where the lessons for Europe become particularly urgent.

    Progressives in France and Spain are right to seek ways of challenging the far-right’s online influence and they should study Janones’ successes, understand his methods and improve their own digital communication, but they should also recognise that winning an election and building a democratic political movement are fundamentally different objectives.

    The temptation to transform electoral mobilisation into permanent political discipline is particularly dangerous for a left that claims to defend pluralism, collective organisation and popular participation. European progressives should not mistake the ability to command millions of followers for the ability to represent them.

    Ultimately, the greatest danger is not that the left will become identical to the far right by adopting its communication techniques, but rather that in its obsession with defeating the far-right, it may begin treating democratic disagreement as an obstacle rather than a principle worth defending.

    The left cannot defend democracy against the far right by narrowing democratic debate within its own ranks.

    ]]>         Listen: What will it take to make the EU’s next budget work? https://euobserver.com/251763/listen-what-will-it-take-to-make-the-eus-next-budget-work/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 10:14:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251763 European leaders are meeting today with one big issue on the table: how much money the EU should have at its disposal over the next seven years, and where that money should go.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    European leaders are meeting today with one big issue on the table: how much money the EU should have at its disposal over the next seven years, and where that money should go.

    And while we shouldn’t expect a deal just yet, the discussions could give us a clearer picture of where Europe is heading, and who might end up paying for it.

    MFF is the acronym for the EU’s Multiannual Financial Framework. The next one will run from 2028 to 2034. If you’ve ever followed the tough negotiations in EU countries over their annual budgets, you can only imagine how difficult it is for 27 countries to agree on a seven-year budget.

    So, today’s and tomorrow’s gathering of EU leaders is just one of many meetings aimed at reaching an agreement on the MFF. This time, the goal is to narrow the gap between the 27 countries and hopefully pave the way for a deal in December.

    Because the question isn’t simply how much money Europe should spend. It’s also about what the EU should prioritise, and how it should pay for it.

    Last Saturday (21 November)), European council president António Costa put forward a new proposal to try to bring countries closer together. Unfortunately, it might not convince everyone just yet.

    Read more

    Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit

    Reactions have been mixed. Many governments, particularly in southern and eastern Europe, want to protect existing spending, especially on agriculture and regional development.

    Others want the EU to invest more in industrial development, innovation and competitiveness. And there are also countries that are simply reluctant to see the overall budget increase, or to contribute more money.

    Costa’s proposal tries to strike a balance between these competing demands. He therefore proposes to reduce the overall size of the budget compared with the Commission’s initial proposal, while introducing new sources of revenue for the EU, so that member states don’t have to shoulder the entire financial burden themselves.

    The problem is always: where do you cut? In the latest proposal, the biggest reductions would affect the competitiveness part of the budget. That’s a sensitive issue because European leaders have spent the past few years insisting that Europe needs to invest more in its economy, support businesses and innovation, and compete with the US and China.

    Read more

    [Interview] Europe’s next budget risks ‘making the strong stronger’ by diverting funds from poorer areas, EU regions chief warns

    But at the same time, there are very few areas where governments are willing to cut spending. Agriculture and regional development, for instance, remain particularly sensitive. These are funds that many countries see as essential to supporting farmers, local economies and regions that are struggling economically.

    So, reducing spending on competitiveness may be a way of finding compromises elsewhere. But it also raises questions about whether Europe will have enough money to deliver on its ambitions.

    The parliament is also pushing for a more ambitious budget, arguing that the EU needs more resources to deal with the challenges ahead.

    And that brings us to another part of Costa’s proposal: how to generate more money for the EU.

    One of the options he has put forward is a digital tax. The idea is to introduce a three percent tax on certain large companies operating in Europe. It would apply to companies with an annual global turnover of more than €750m and more than €50m in turnover in the EU from digital activities.

    Read more

    With no summit deal expected, it is clear the EU budget falls short on ambition – but does it matter?

    We’re talking mainly about large tech companies. Smaller European firms, such as Mistral AI, would not fall under these thresholds, at least for now. This tax could generate around €5bln a year, or roughly €35bln over the seven-year budget period.

    That would help finance the EU budget without relying entirely on additional contributions from national governments. But getting the 27 countries to agree on a new tax is no easy task.

    Some countries, particularly Ireland, are concerned that taxing large tech companies could make Europe less attractive to investors and encourage businesses to move elsewhere. There are also fears of potential retaliation from the United States.

    Still, this digital tax is one of the options considered most likely to gain support among member states.

    We’ll have to wait, probably a few more weeks, to see whether this tax makes its way into the final agreement.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/26/brazil-china-react-to-new-trump-tariffs-threat</link>
      <description><p>Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/trump-new-china-tariffs-europe">Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU</a></p></li></ul><p>Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.</p><p>Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits.       <title>Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses</link>
      <description><p>Federal judge Loren L AliKhan grants preliminary injunction in ABC’s favor after network sued FCC in August</p><p>The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/18/abc-sues-trump-federal-communications-commission">sued the agency</a> in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.</p><p>The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Total number of drivers dropped 5% over the last year and fell 15% compared with 2019 levels, new report finds</p><p>The number of school bus drivers in the US has dropped 5% over the last year as drivers continue to experience low pay, poor working conditions and school budget shortfalls, according to a new report.</p><p>The total number of school bus drivers is down 15%, or nearly 34,000 drivers, compared with 2019 levels, according to an new <a href="https://www.epi.org/blog/the-school-bus-driver-shortage-is-worsening-as-wages-fall-once-again/#_ref2">analysis</a> from the Economic Policy Institute.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/nov/24/school-bus-driver-decline-budget">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/nvidia-staff-what-do-you-think-jensen-huang-return-chief-executive">Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?</a></p></li></ul><p>One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/23/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-chief-executive">reinstated</a> Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.</p><p>But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/06/folarin-balogun-red-card-reversal-trump-calls-fifa-explainer">Folarin Balogun</a> after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Amid air chaos, travelers will have to navigate an outdated system (and complex company policies if it all goes wrong)</p><p>Millions of people are planning to fly in the US over the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the US Federal Aviation Administration’s 13 November <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">ground stop</a> halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11 (aside from a brief halt in 2023).</p><p>In the chaos that ensued, some travelers embarked on <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/royalcaribbean/comments/1xvkopq/comment/19smxjywidlcw/?context=3">overnight drives</a> to catch cruise ships and <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/women-stranded-faa-ground-stop-buy-ford-bronco-27-hour-road-trip-rcna609629">bought new cars</a> to make business meetings. Many had to simply cancel their plans and incur the costs that came with it. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled at a potential cost to travelers of $1.9bn in lost time and related expenses, <a href="https://www.andersoneconomicgroup.com/analysis-nationwide-ground-stop-cost-travelers-nearly-2-billion/">Anderson Economic Group estimates</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer">Continue reading...</a></description>
