<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 27 Nov 2026 10:32:12 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Revolut vs Zippay: Who is winning the battle for the Irish wallet?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/27/neobanks-vs-trad-banks-who-is-winning-the-battle-for-the-irish-wallet/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/27/neobanks-vs-trad-banks-who-is-winning-the-battle-for-the-irish-wallet/Fri, 27 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000On paper, the Irish banks appear outgunned in the world of neobanks and digital finance platforms.

Revolut – once a foreign upstart with a novelty feature that allowed users to split their restaurant bills with one another – now bestrides much of the globe and leads the way in digital banking.

The London-headquartered fintech says it now serves more than 80 million customers across 40 countries. That includes 3.4 million customers in Ireland.

Last year, it reported revenues of $6 billion and in October was valued at $115 billion – making it bigger than Barclays and Societe Generale.

Most pertinently for the main lenders here – it says that 80 per cent of Irish adults have a Revolut account.

And in a move with no little symbolic importance, Revolut last week announced it had signed a 10-year lease for office space in the old Ulster Bank headquarters in Dublin’s south quays.

The so-called pillar banks, AIB, Bank of Ireland and PTSB, spent much of the past decade looking on as Revolut set about attempting to dominate the personal transaction space in Ireland.

The household name in digital banking has now been joined here by the likes of Monzo, which launched in Ireland in April and offers fee-free personal and banking accounts.

Irish users are well accustomed with splitting bills, sending money to friends and relatives and paying for all manner of children’s sporting activities with Revolut’s peer-to-peer payment system.

Yet, it was only this year that the traditional Irish banks were able to roll out a feature that would emulate this key function. Launched in March, the Irish banking establishment’s response was called Zippay.

It had been a relatively long road to fruition, with an earlier effort falling by the wayside in 2023.

As Revolut attracted new Irish users during Covid in 2020, the banks unveiled their plans for Synch.

The company, set up by AIB, Bank of Ireland, PTSB and the now departed KBC Ireland, started work on its own stand-alone payment app called Yippay.

Within three years, having butted heads with regulators along the way, the banks recognised that the instant payments landscape had changed and Yippay was no more.

The whole plan was not scrapped, however. The technology, provided by Italian paytech company Nexi, was repurposed so that it could be incorporated directly into existing banking apps and Zippay was born.

So how has it been faring and has it helped the banks retain account holders?

“They had to do it,” says Anastasia Turdyeva, Dublin-based director of financial institutions ratings at S&P Global Ratings.

“Almost everyone in Ireland has Revolut – it has been there for years and people have got used to it”. Zippay, she says, “is not yet at full speed” but is well designed and easy to use.

“The volumes are growing. I think in a year’s time it will be more clear if it is on an upward trend,” she says.

The biggest impediment to sustained growth in use of the payment system, says Turdyeva, is that people are accustomed to using Revolut and it enjoys the advantage of being the first to market.

When asked if its members could produce numbers on how many transactions are done using Zippay, the Banking and Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI) said it was unable to do so.

However, Central Bank of Ireland figures published last month point to a significant change in consumer behaviour, which has been attributed to the new service.

Card spending on financial services fell by more than €600 million, around a third, in August compared to the same month last year.

“This significant decline likely reflects a shift in payment preference rather than reduced consumer spending,” said the Central Bank. “The introduction of account-to-account (A2A) banking services such as Zippay by Irish banks has provided consumers with an alternative payment option.

“Consequently, these transactions are no longer recorded as card payments, explaining the sharp decline in card-based financial services spending.”

Sharon Brennan, head of the BPFI’s collaboration office, said the banks were seeing Zippay usage “grow week on week” and they were currently trying to target a younger cohort across social media platforms.

Zippay needs to play to its natural advantages

“We had a great starting position as the service was made available to all customers of the three banks that had eligible accounts,” she says. “There was no additional registration process for those customers – so we started with a very broad reach from day one.”

Revolut has certainly noticed.

In a meeting with Department of Finance officials in April, its country manager, Malcolm Craig, was reported as saying Zippay gave the traditional banks a “significant competitive advantage”.

However, sources say Craig’s comments were somewhat “throwaway”, and suggest the minutes of the meeting, released under a Freedom of Information request, didn’t represent Revolut’s true position.

“We see [Zippay] as predominantly an alternative – a way for bricks and mortar banks to meet changing customer expectations in the fast-changing world of digital payments,” says Brennan.

“It’s about removing that friction associated with using a traditional Iban [international bank account number] and BIC [bank identifier code]. It removes a huge pain point for customers.”

She says there were a number of regulatory challenges faced by Synch and Yippay that meant the process of bringing a payments service to market took longer – but also the marketplace was changing.

“It just came to a point when everybody had to stand back and look at the way the world was moving,” she says. “We needed to pivot – and that steered us towards going within-app as opposed to offering a stand-alone app”.

Revolut maintains that its transaction volumes have not been impacted since the launch of Zippay – it recently suggested they may have even increased a little since then. A statement in September said the number of peer-to-peer payments “despite the advent of new, direct competition – has continued to rise”.

Lessons from Ireland’s Revolut revolution

The bank says 86 per cent of its Irish customers use the app every month. Revolut does not comment publicly on Zippay.

“It’s tough to know [how widespread use of Zippay is] – it’s a bit of smoke and daggers,” says Darragh Cassidy of the price comparison website Bonkers.ie.

“From an anecdotal point of view, sometimes it is easier to just Zippay someone – you don’t have to top up your app like with Revolut. Now, the user interface isn’t as good – when I send money with PTSB I always feel there is an extra step required.

“When I tell people I’m using Zippay – the reaction is still a little bit ‘What’? I think it is an okay service – a little bit simpler. But for a lot of younger people, who don’t have bank accounts or don’t want one, they are going to be using Revolut constantly.”

It is this generational divide that Revolut will have to now bet on if it wants to crack the truly profitable parts of the Irish market – mortgages and loans. Getting to this point will mean making proper inroads in the current-account market.

I don’t think there is a risk to the established banks from Revolut when it comes to mortgages

Dmitry Nazarov, S&P

Cassidy points to recent figures – such as those contained in a Consumer Sentiment Banking Survey last month – that showed only 6 per cent of Revolut users here identify it as their main account.

“If you ask people: ‘Do you use Revolut?’ And they’ll say, ‘Yes, I do’. Ask them: ‘Do you get paid into your account?’ – and the answer is no. People tend to keep their bank accounts,” he says.

The analysts are very much aware of this.

S&P’s primary credit analyst for Revolut, Dmitry Nazarov, says gaining a higher degree of “primacy” in the Irish current account market is one of the company’s main aims.

“It’s part of a strategy to strengthen and deepen customer relationships across their core markets,” he says. “We see some positive dynamic there – in terms of engagement – but over the past two years the trajectory has been relatively slow.”

The rationale behind capturing a large segment of the deposit market is to provide a foothold that might then enable the digital bank to move into mortgages and personal loans.

Nazarov foresees little real challenge to the traditional banks in the short term.

“Revolut has a very, very small mortgage portfolio,” he says. “It has nothing in Ireland. The mortgage market is quite different in terms of [regulatory] requirements and the infrastructure they will need to build. I think it’s going to be a very long way for them.

“I don’t think there is [a] risk to the established banks from Revolut when it comes to mortgages.”

Against this background, Revolut announced in September that its Irish credit portfolio had surpassed the €1 billion threshold. It said that having achieved that in just over four years underlined the success of its “play for mainstream market share in Ireland” and that almost a tenth of its Irish customer base was borrowing from it.

It’s understood the company is still intent on bringing mortgages to the Irish market and regards them as a priority but there is no clear time line on when this might happen.

As for suggestions that the bank has fallen behind on its overall strategy of growing lending, sources point to recent comments made by Revolut founder Nik Storonsky who said he wanted it to be a bank with “effectively zero risk”.

Storonsky said that while traditional lenders would loan out 100 per cent of their deposits, Revolut would maintain a much lower loan-to-deposit rate.

Revolut’s model, said the Russian-born entrepreneur, was designed to target the most profitable segments of consumer finance – and leave the risky, capital-intensive investment decisions to the older financial institutions.

“Revolut has been very clear that they are going to be selective in their lending business,” says Navarov. “All of the lending growth has been very fast – with the loan portfolio almost doubling every year – but they started from a very low base”.

Turdyeva agrees that there is little imminent threat to the Irish banks from Revolut’s lending plans – but that they need to be aware of what future banking customers, brought up with Revolut and other similar digital banks, will expect in terms of service.

“The fundamentals of the Irish banks are very strong and they have good positioning for a number of years ahead,” says the banking analyst. “What they need to think about is future competition and generational change.

Navro chief Joe Redmond: ‘I don’t quite fit the profile of a fintech start-up CEO at this stage in my career’

“Other services could be considered by Revolut – there are other things where Revolut can be competitive such as investment – it’s still evolving in Ireland.

“Revolut and Monzo are becoming more visible in the space with products other than just payment services. BankInter came into the area a year ago – these guys will also be more active.”

She points to the Government’s Savings and Investment Accounts, which are to be launched next year, as a potential opportunity for Revolut to grow its share of the Irish market. Many users of the Revolut app will be aware that it already enables users to dabble in stock and crypto trading.

“I think this is on the agenda for the domestic banks,” she says. “They are definitely mindful of generational change and preferences. They’ve put a lot of investment into making their apps more appealing. Time will tell – but so far the story is one of being very resilient”.

As for Zippay, it is understood that the Irish banks intend to expand its offering over the coming months. The introduction of QR-code facilities and small-merchant features are thought to be under consideration. This would allow bank customers to use Zippay to quickly buy coffees and other small items.

Sharon Brennan of the BPFI, meanwhile, says Nexi – the provider of Zippay’s software – is “actively engaging” with other Irish financial institutions with a view to rolling it out further.

It’s understood Revolut is not among them – and has no plans on joining. In the meantime, the battle for Irish wallets continues.

]]><![CDATA[An Post chief Fergal Leamy: ‘It’s a business that’s very fragile. It hasn’t made a profit since 2019’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/27/its-a-business-thats-very-fragile-it-hasnt-made-a-profit-since-2019/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/27/its-a-business-thats-very-fragile-it-hasnt-made-a-profit-since-2019/Fri, 27 Nov 2026 05:59:00 +0000“Is this the ninth floor?” inquires An Post’s new chief executive, Fergal Leamy, as he pokes his head out of the lift.

We’re a floor shy, as it happens. You’d think he’d know given that’s where his office is located. It takes two lifts to reach there from the An Post reception in the Exo building in Dublin’s north docks that houses the company’s headquarters.

To be fair, he’s spent much of his first three months with the State-owned company on the road, visiting its various post offices, sorting hubs, delivery centres and depots to meet its staff, get a feel for how the business operates and the challenges he now faces as its chief executive.

As we sip some hot refreshments from high-backed chairs in An Post’s shade of green, Leamy is very clear about what lies ahead.

“It has wonderful assets, wonderful people, fabulous stuff done over the last while but it’s not a sustainable business yet,” he says.

“It’s a business that’s very fragile, it’s a business that hasn’t made a profit since 2019. We’ve grown revenue by 20 per cent since 2019 but we’re still loss-making. That’s where the fragility is.

“So how do we make it a sustainable business over the long term? With some of the inherent structural issues ... mail is still half of our revenue and that is going to continue to decline. The challenge is to get profitable growth over the next period of time.

“We’re in a great position given our market share in parcels and logistics and our presence on distributed financial products and our ability to impact on every part of the country. But it’s about making choices about how we go after that.”

Leamy is currently trying to formulate a new five-year strategy out to 2032, which will be presented around the end of the first quarter next year.

He says An Post ranks about 27th out of 32 postal services groups in profitability globally. He cites Nordic and Austrian postal operators who hit a return of 5 to 10 per cent earnings before interest and tax (ebit).

On the other end of the scale, the US postal operator is heavily loss-making, while PostNord in Denmark axed its letters business at the end of last year.

In 2019, An Post’s ebit was €41 million. It moved to a loss during the Covid years while last year it was minus €7 million. Leamy expects it to be another minus of between €6 million and €7 million this year.

Huge capital expenditure is required by An Post in the coming years to facilitate growth in its parcels business, including €200 million on a national parcels centre that it will locate (subject to planning approval) at Grange Castle in Dublin.

“There will be the digitisation of the organisation to make it fit for purpose, which will be significant, and there will be further changes across our portfolio that we need to invest in. In order to do that we need to be generating profits and cash,” he says.

Overall, the capital investment required over the next five years will be “at least” €300 million.

In its favour, the Government has agreed to lift An Post’s borrowing cap from €74.3 million to €620 million. That’s still subject to legislative changes that he hopes will come in at the end of the year.

While it gives the State-owned postal group significant financial headroom, the money still needs to be paid back, hence his focus on reshaping it into a profitable, sustainable entity into the long term.

He says the payback from the national parcels centre should be “phenomenal”.

“It allows us to dramatically reduce the cost of the middle mile [the sorting of letters and parcels] section of our business.”

A new facility opened recently at Cheeverstown in Dublin as an interim measure, with 50 people per shift over three shifts a day. “One site can now handle 100,000 parcels a day, which is incremental for us. In our peak week this year, we will do 3.4 million parcels and now we have the capacity to do that.

“With a national parcels centre, we will have the capacity to do significantly more without the need for significantly more people. That’s very cost efficient and the return on investment for us will be really significant. It could take as much as €25 million to €40 million a year out of our cost base.”

Potentially, the new parcels centre could process up to five million packages a week, he says. “At the moment we can probably do four million a week from our current sites. We will consolidate some of our sites but this would allow us to do seven to eight million items in total.”

He says parcel volumes are growing at 20 to 25 per cent a year, so “this will be needed”. Even if ecommerce growth slows, he says the centre will offer efficiency gains for the company.

At present, An Post has about 11,000 employees. Leamy doesn’t expect that number to “change dramatically” although the nature of the roles will alter, with more people working in the afternoon or evening and across weekends.

“We’ve hired a temporary workforce of 350 in the past few months to satisfy demand this year. Parcels are bulky and a different business. We’ll have an overhead that’s appropriate for the business we need to do.”

At present, An Post has about 9,500 frontline staff (including postmen and women) with another 1,400 in head office and support roles. Leamy suggests there might be fewer support staff and more frontline ones in the years ahead.

“These are the things we’ll have to look at. At the moment we’re still loss making and we need to be as efficient or more efficient as any new player coming into the market.”

This is the first job I’ve had where my largest customers have a strategy to move away from us. But that’s the truth – people are digitising

He cites the example of its €105 million annual spend on running costs for its fleet of vehicles. “You go to any depot today and you’ll see them being used for about five hours, so you can imagine the efficiency if we can sweat those assets in a more efficient way. We need to figure this all out.”

Leamy says growth is there if An Post wants it and cites strong relationships with ecommerce customers, such as Marks & Spencer, Eason, Amazon and SMEs around the country.

“If we don’t change they all have other options if they’re not satisfied with our service,” he says. “If they’re not happy, they’ll move to DPD, or UPS or others.

“We have to set ourselves up to be as efficient as they are. And the unions know this better than me. They get it that for the 11,000 employees and 11,000 pensioners this needs to be sustainable and needs to be self-financing.”

Regarding letters, volumes declined by 11.5 per cent in October, he says. “Last year was down 10.5 per cent. This is the first job I’ve had where my largest customers have a strategy to move away from us. But that’s the truth – people are digitising.”

This includes the banks, Government agencies and Revenue. “It’s the right thing for them to do. But that has an impact on us. So we need to be close to our customers to understand their plans to manage the decline on the letters side.”

Four Irish authors honoured with stamps celebrating their work

Stamp prices have risen consistently over the past decade to a current rate of €1.85 for a standard letter but Leamy says “you can’t do that forever” and you’d reach the point where volumes are so small it would have little financial impact.

The State still requires An Post to deliver letters every day to every house, something that Leamy says needs to change.

“There are a couple of options, every second day or every third day. Or different pricing strategies for next-day delivery versus standard. Most people are more interested in next-day delivery of parcels than letters.

“As a country we need to have that conversation. That’s something we intend to do next year, ideally making that change in 2028. We’re engaged with Government, with stakeholders and with ComReg. We need to grasp the nettle. We can’t just keep kicking the can down the road.”

I do like the personal touch of sending a thank-you letter to someone. And I’m actually now at the stage of sending condolences via letter

Leamy accepts that is an ambitious timescale but argues there is “no option to move slowly”, adding that the incremental annual costs are €30 million to €40 million.

“We would redeploy that resource to growing our business elsewhere,” he adds.

He accepts that some of the changes will be “unpopular” and “battles lie ahead” but “ultimately the direction of travel is clear”.

An Post generates €600 million-plus in revenue from letters today but could lose about half of that over the next five to seven years, he predicts.

“In many ways it would be easier if it went to zero because you could plan for it but, look, it will still be €300 million or so of income.”

When did he last send a letter, a postcard or a birthday greeting by post?

“About two or three days ago,” he says with a chuckle, adding that before he joined An Post it was probably every couple or months.

“I’ll have to do it more often now. I do like the personal touch of sending a thank-you letter to someone. And I’m actually now at the stage of sending condolences via letter now as well.”

While letters are down, footfall has risen in post offices this year, he says, due to the impact of Vinted, an online marketplace for second-hand items.

“We have a whole cohort of new customers coming to our post offices now. The average age is 16 to 28 for Vinted customers, largely female. If we’d done a strategy three years ago, we would have missed that.”

What impact has the recent introduction of charges for non-EU parcels had on volumes?

“Week one in July, we saw a dip of about 200,000 parcels in a week. By week three, we saw no change in the volumes. But where they are coming from has dramatically changed. The Asian players have been smart to react and have set up warehouses in various European countries. But the UK has been significantly impacted from this. The volume has dramatically changed,” he says, adding that items are now being shipped here by companies via continental Europe rather than Britain.

“This has had more impact than Brexit. The switching that’s going on through France and Germany is phenomenal.”

New €2 charge for online shoppers – what you need to know

This is Leamy’s second stint as a chief executive in the State sector, having previously spent 4½ years with forestry group Coillte.

Between times, he was a senior executive (including a stint as CEO) at the successful family-owned Glen Dimplex business, controlled by the Naughton family, having joined in mid-2019.

“It’s a fascinating business ... and it was quite intense because we did a lot of restructuring. There were areas where we couldn’t compete but there’s a thriving business there now.”

He left in June 2025.

Before Coillte, Leamy had spent about 15 years abroad in various roles, including a lucrative stint in private equity. He returned to Ireland with his family in 2015 and is happy to no longer spend 70 to 90 nights a year away from his family on work.

“It wears on you, there’s no doubt about that,” he says.

He’s delighted to have settled in Dublin. “Dublin is not far off being a phenomenal city. Having worked around the world, it has the right balance of education and sports facilities, you can be on the water if that’s your thing, you can go walking in the mountains or for a run. Very few cities can do that.”

Despite only being in his late 40s, Leamy’s successful career meant he didn’t necessarily need another full-time role on departing Glen Dimplex, but An Post tempted him.

“When I stepped down from Glen Dimplex, I wasn’t certain I was going to do something full-time again. I was quite happy being on boards, investing and doing different things.

“When I heard David [McRedmond, his predecessor at An Post] was stepping down this grabbed me in terms of a curious challenge. It’s got some real challenges ahead of it as an organisation.

“A lot of people sit on the fence and give opinions. I challenged myself to get stuck in and do something. I want to bounce out of bed in the morning to tackle the challenge. And that’s what this does.”

He accepts the role is not without jeopardy, although it’s hard to imagine An Post being allowed to go out of business, regardless of the challenges it faces.

There is also the question of State ownership. Is that the right structure for An Post?

“That’s a question for another day. I don’t have a solid view. There are many different models around the world. Our job as managers is to get the business into the best possible shape for its current shareholders.”

Will this be his last full-time gig? “For me, it’s always been about the challenge and the opportunity. I will always be busy, it’s just the form it takes.”

By the end of his seven years at An Post, what does he hope to have achieved? “To describe this as a sustainable business, and not just from a climate perspective. A business that can sustain itself going forward. Today it can’t. A business that can stand on its own two feet and isn’t worrying about the decline in letters.”

CV

Name: Fergal Leamy.

Job: An Post chief executive.

Age: 49.

Lives: Donnybrook, Dublin 4.

Family: Married with three children, ranging in ages from nine up to 18.

Hobbies: “Massively into sports, playing golf and padel and cycling. And watching lots of sports.” He’s a Tottenham Hotspur fan.

Something you might expect: “I like getting out to see how a business actually works – in An Post that means sorting and delivery units and post offices. The frontline people doing the work tell you pretty quickly what’s making their day harder, and what we could do better.”

Something that might surprise: “About 15 years ago I was the second-largest farmer in Australia, running 400,000 head of cattle across 5.7 million hectares of land.”

Leadership style: “I’m a big believer in serve and support, building teams, empowering teams and then supporting them to deliver. I have a strong awareness of my limitations and I’m a big fan of getting people around you who are empowered and can get on with things.”

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[Stocks extend recovery on AI trade rebound]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/27/stocks-extend-recovery-on-ai-trade-rebound/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/27/stocks-extend-recovery-on-ai-trade-rebound/Fri, 27 Nov 2026 08:41:06 +0000Investors piled back into equities at the end of the week as the AI trade rebounded and China stepped up support for its stock market.

MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 1.8 per cent, building on a rebound that began on Wall Street Wednesday after the Nasdaq 100 Index briefly slipped into bear-market territory. Shares in mainland China rallied more than 4 per cent after the State Council reaffirmed its support for the market.

]]>Neustockimages<![CDATA[Would you tell an AI interviewer what you really think?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/27/would-you-tell-an-ai-interviewer-what-you-really-think/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/27/would-you-tell-an-ai-interviewer-what-you-really-think/Fri, 27 Nov 2026 06:01:00 +0000An awful lot of time and money in the 21st century is spent trying to find out what people think: about politicians; about products; about companies; about just about anything. Consider the UK’s long-running Skills and Employment Survey, which has been performed via face-to-face interviews every five years or so since the 1980s in an attempt to trace people’s experiences of work. In 2024, the researchers conducted a parallel survey online to see if the responses would be consistent with the original method. They found evidence of what Francis Green, a University College London emeritus professor who works on the survey, calls “social esteem bias”: respondents were sometimes more positive, or less negative, when asked in person by a fellow human.

The face-to-face method, for example, found that 17 per cent of Britons were dissatisfied with their jobs in 2012, while 14 per cent said the same in 2024. But the web survey responses in 2024 portrayed the workforce in a much grumpier mood: 23 per cent said they were dissatisfied.

This is a potential problem for those who collect data for long time series, many of whom are keen to shift to online survey methods because of rising costs and falling response rates for face-to-face interviews. But an even more profound methodological change is in the offing in certain parts of the research world.

Unlike big surveys with thousands of respondents, qualitative research involves long, in-depth interviews that illuminate some of the nuance and richness of people’s thoughts and experiences (but – due to their cost – on a necessarily small scale). Now, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has opened a new possibility: that chatbots could allow researchers to combine the scale of quantitative data with the richness of qualitative data.

Would we answer questions differently if AI were doing the asking? And if so, how? Nesta, a UK innovation agency, has conducted a series of small, careful experiments with AI in qualitative research over the past few years. At first, they found that AI interviewers solicited short and thin answers from humans. Some respondents even used ChatGPT themselves to look up the “right” answers.

But the technology has advanced since then – in particular, people can now answer via “voice notes” rather than having to type. Mallory Durran, Nesta’s chief technology officer, told me that those who were sceptical about AI still tended to give quite “short or direct” answers, but others found it to be “less judgmental [and] it was actually easier [to share experiences] when you’re not looking into the eyes of another human”.

The other advantage is that people can talk to AI interviewers in whichever language they’re most comfortable in. “Where we’re working with people in a second language, so not in English, you get way more back than we did with face-to-face interviews,” Durran said. “It seems to be really opening the floodgate.”

In other words, AI interviewers might solicit less information from some people, but much more from others. In particular, the technology could allow researchers to gather the experiences of those who have traditionally been hard to reach, particularly because of language barriers. But it won’t solve every old problem (plenty of hard-to-reach people are also digitally disconnected) and will create some new ones.

For my money, the biggest danger will be in the temptation to scale up and up and up. To give an example, Anthropic last year used Claude to interview more than 80,000 people about their AI use across 159 countries in what it called “the largest and most multilingual qualitative study ever conducted”.

Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang

Once AI is gathering so much data, the next temptation – indeed, probably a practical necessity – will be to use it to read and analyse all those interview transcripts too. That could result in a scenario where human researchers don’t conduct the interviews, or even read the answers people give, but instead receive some smooth, machine-processed analysis of what lies beneath. As a result, they would be far less connected to the messy, nuanced complexity of what people had to say. And when it comes to qualitative research, isn’t that the whole point?

It’s a danger that extends beyond this realm, I suspect: we may become so enamoured of our bigger, faster, newly mechanised methods that we forget what we actually wanted to achieve in the first place. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

It’s these “other obligations” that are making markets jittery.

These arrangements let companies with strong credit positions support weaker-credit firms to finance projects “without having an immediate, direct effect on the balance sheets of the stronger-credit firms”.

Pension funds vary but Aidan Donnelly, head of global equities at Davy, points out that a pension fund would typically have 55 to 60 per cent invested in equities on average.

The US would typically account for 65 per cent of this index and, to take one example, Nvidia has a market weight of about 6 per cent so it might represent 2-2½ per cent-plus of a typical pension fund.

Figures produced by the pension industry for individual funds confirm this and in some cases the holdings are higher. In the Irish Life Forum 4 fund, for example, a typical mid- to higher-risk product which would be used to build up investment with retirement still a way off, the top 10 equities – all major US companies except for Taiwan Semiconductor – account for 24 per cent of the total fund value.

Five big US firms – Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, account for 18 per cent, with Apple and Nvidia both at about 4.5 per cent. This has paid off this year, with the fund up close to 10 per cent to date despite the recent fall-off in US equities. And the rise in these shares has been stellar over the past few years with Nvidia rising from $50 three years ago to almost $150 now.

But the concentration risk of pension funds to these big players is there, nonetheless. And obviously the risk for those invested outside their pension in US-linked investment funds which match the big indices is all the greater.

The dollar bounce

The US dollar has risen against the euro this year – by close to 7 per cent. This has given a big bounce to Irish pension funds invested in the US when dollar investments are translated back to euro. Donnelly of Davys points out that despite the latest fall-off in US shares from their highs, the annual returns are still generally in double figures in euro terms. In turn this has been a big support to Irish pension funds this year.

The S&P 500 is up by close to 5 per cent from January but add in the impact of the rising US dollar and this brings the total gain in euro terms to about 12 per cent. This gain was 16 per cent in September, but the annual return is still very healthy for investors on this side of the Atlantic. Many Irish pension funds from the main providers are up 10-15 per cent year to date and even more cautious ones are up 7 to 10 per cent.

The AI risk

With funds heavily invested in the AI bubble and the wider US economy which depends on it, it is self-evident that there is a risk if the bubble “bursts”, or even if the more gentle generally downward trend in share prices seen in recent weeks were to continue.

Big international investment houses now publishing their outlooks for 2027 remain broadly upbeat, though conscious of the risks. UBS Securities, for example, says it believes investors should “stay in the market”, though concentrate on diversifying their portfolios in an environment of “elevated uncertainty”.

This uncertainty involves the much-discussed issue of whether the returns from AI will justify investor enthusiasm. With AI investment in the US set to rise, on UBS estimates from $1 trillion in 2026 – the bulk of which comes from the big players – to $1.6 trillion next year, the question is what return this will show and how quickly this will become evident.

If investment continues to outpace returns, investor fears will grow, as we have seen in recent weeks.

This poses a risk for pensions going into 2027. So too does the environment of rising interest rates, which could – if it worsens – lead to falls in the value of bond holdings, another mainstay of pensions. In 2022, both equities and bonds fell together, the nightmare scenario for funds.

But since then returns have been strong and even allowing for 2022 five-year returns for many funds are 20 to 30 per cent.

Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang

The point is that pensions are a longer-term investment and, as Donnelly points out, this means pension holders face volatility but this does not necessarily add up to risk. Someone who has chosen a more aggressive fund and is hoping to buy an annuity may be exposed, but most managed funds will lower risk close to retirement.

And increasingly those taking their pension do so via a vehicle such as an approved retirement fund which means they will remain invested in the market, rather than leaving themselves exposed to the value of their fund on the one day they buy an annuity.

None of this removes the cost of a bursting of the AI bubble – if it happens – to your pension fund which would take time to recoup. It would lead to a painful fall in value. When the dot.com bubble burst in 2000, the S&P 500 dropped 50 per cent in the next two years, as the US fell into recession following the 9/11 attacks and Irish pension funds had two bad years.

There followed a period of strong gains before the 2008 financial crisis. The point is that over the longer term the averages should work in favour of pension investors.

The story of the markets and the US economy in the last few years, as UBS points out, is one of resilience – but nobody knows where the AI story is going.

The State savings scheme

A final thought on the new State savings scheme, due to launch in the middle of next year. The funds which Irish investors will be offered will offer various levels of risk, but the higher-risk ones will be weighted towards equities.

While people understand that their pension funds are longer-term investments, do they realise they need the same mindset for these funds – not that they are saving for retirement, but that equity investing by its nature carries risks and that “needing” the money back at a specific point in, say, a year’s time is a risky strategy?

]]>Eric Luke<![CDATA[Irish housing wealth now close to €1tn]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/irish-housing-wealth-now-close-to-1-trillion/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/irish-housing-wealth-now-close-to-1-trillion/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:59:11 +0000

Irish households now own nearly a €1 trillion worth of property assets, according to the Central Bank.

The regulator’s latest wealth report indicated that housing accounted for 67 per cent – or €956 billion – of the €1.43 trillion in wealth held by households here in the second quarter.

The total net wealth figure represents “a new series high,” the bank said.

It equates to about €245,000 per person, or €724,000 per household.

The wealth of households has risen in tandem with house prices which have doubled in a decade.

The latest quarterly was, however, driven by a rise in financial assets of €35.3 billion, with “positive revaluations” accounting for most of the increase.

Housing wealth increased by €11 billion over the quarter, also due to positive revaluations.

The net wealth of households is calculated by adding the total value of the housing stock and financial assets – such as cash savings, shares, pensions and possessions such as cars and antiques – and subtracting debt owed or liabilities.

It is considered a crude measure of prosperity as it hides the distribution of household assets and liabilities across income groups and age categories.

The latest figures highlight a very uneven distribution of wealth in Ireland, with the total net wealth of households in the poorest half of the distribution accounting for less than 10 per cent (€145 billion) of the national total.

By contrast, the top 10 per cent of Irish households owned €686.7 billion, 47 per cent, of total household net wealth in the State.

“As a result, the wealthiest 10 per cent of Irish households continued to hold nearly five times the amount held by households in the bottom half of the net wealth distribution all together,” the bank said.

Households in the middle part of the income distribution (deciles six to nine) owned €629.4 billion overall, or 43.1 per cent of total net wealth.

The balance-sheet composition of Irish households also differed significantly depending on the income level.

Households in the top 10 per cent net wealth decile displayed a more diversified portfolio composition with other financial assets (comprising debt securities, listed shares, investment fund shares and life insurance and annuity entitlements) featuring “prominently”, accounting for 19.4 per cent of total assets.

The bank also noted that wealthier households also displayed lower leverage (meaning they had less debt) when compared with households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution.

Conversely, households in the lower deciles held their financial wealth mainly in deposits (18.5 per cent of their total assets) and were significantly more leveraged (28.1 per cent).

Ella Gleeson, private client manager with wealth advisers NFP Ireland, said: “While today’s report shows that household wealth continues to rise in Ireland, increasing by almost €43 billion, rising living costs are putting pressure on disposable incomes and could make it harder for families to save, invest and build their wealth.

“Today’s report shows that a significant proportion of Irish household wealth is tied up in property,” she added. “While rising property values can make families wealthier on paper, that does not necessarily mean they have greater financial resilience.”

]]>Nathan Laine<![CDATA[Can my brother move into our elderly father’s house before our inheritance is finalised?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/can-my-brother-move-into-our-elderly-fathers-house-before-our-inheritance-is-finalised/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/can-my-brother-move-into-our-elderly-fathers-house-before-our-inheritance-is-finalised/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Q: A reader and his two siblings are to inherit their father’s home and savings in equal shares; he has told them so. But with their father, who is experiencing dementia, now in a nursing home, the siblings are worried about the house being empty. Could they rent it out?

The siblings are in agreement with a brother’s plan to move into the house when he retires and their father has died. He would buy out the other two. But could the brother move in now, settling up with his siblings later from the proceeds of the will?

“If this person was in my consultation room, the very first priority is to go home and find the insurance policy,” says Andrea Clarke, principal solicitor at Coyne Solicitors.

“If the property isn’t insured and it burns down, there is no asset,” says Clarke.

The insurer will need to be informed that the house is unoccupied.

The reader’s father was an organised man. As well as sharing his will with his children, he registered an enduring power of attorney (EPA). The reader is the trusted person he appointed to make decisions on his behalf.

This EPA is now being enacted, the reader says. But the EPA alone may not give his son the power to rent out the property or allow his brother to move in.

My mother got an inheritance and a gift from her parents – can she reduce her tax bill?

“Your obligation first and foremost is to carry out the father’s wishes in his will and under the EPA,” says Clarke.

The primary concern should be their father’s care now.

“There is no entitlement for the children to have the house until the father passes away.

“You can’t make decisions in relation to the house or give it to a brother unless the EPA explicitly permits that,” says Clarke.

The reader may need to get court approval to move forward, says Clarke.

If the court did allow the property to be transferred to the brother, capital acquisitions tax (CAT) and capital gains tax would all have to be dealt with now, she says.

Revenue won’t wait until the father dies to be paid the tax.

If the father is availing of the Fair Deal scheme, where his income and assets contribute to paying for his nursing home, the HSE will have a say too, says Clarke.

The HSE might be quite happy for it to be rented, maximising their return. New rules, however, mean tenancies now run in rolling six-year cycles. A tenancy can only be ended mid-cycle on very limited grounds.

“The death of their father would not be a reason to terminate a lease mid-cycle,” says Clarke. This means the siblings may not get vacant possession of the house when they want it.

Renting it on Airbnb, if the EPA and local planning rules allow it, would be more flexible, but it would entail work.

I’m giving my son a €490,000 property. Can I cut tax bill by giving part of it as a loan?

Another option is to rent the house to the brother, but it would have to be at market rent, says Clarke.

Alternatively, the brother could move into the house under a “caretaker’s agreement”, effectively providing a service to the family by occupying the property, says Clarke.

This would have to be carefully drafted so as not be interpreted as a tenancy that could cause problems if the siblings were to fall out.

The caretaker’s agreement would need to address any EPA or court requirements. The HSE, however, may not want someone living in the property for free when renting it would generate income.

If the brother does move under a caretaker’s agreement, he could then seek dwelling house relief – this would allow him to inherit the house tax-free, without using up his tax-free CAT threshold, says Clarke.

He would need to live in the house as his main residence for the three years immediately before his father’s death and have no beneficial interest in another property, and he must live in the house for six years after he has inherited it, to claim the relief.

Can we continue renting to our Ukrainian friends and reclaim our holiday home later?

“The father could die sooner, he might not get that three-year period,” says Clarke.

If the family does go this route, then when their father dies, they could complete a “deed of family arrangement”, she says.

This isn’t about the siblings changing the will, but changing how the assets are distributed.

“The will says everything gets divided between the three of them, but all the beneficiaries could agree that one brother gets the house and the other two get the money,” says Clarke.

A deed of family arrangement must be completed within two years of their father’s death and before the grant of probate is extracted.

If there isn’t enough money in the estate for everyone to get an equal share, they could agree to an equalisation payment to square things up.

As his father’s personal representative, the reader could alternatively distribute the assets “in specie”, under the rules of appropriation.

Just like the deed of family arrangement, this is not a free hand to rewrite the will, but he could give the house to the brother with the bank savings going to himself and his sister, so long as this is consistent with the beneficiaries rights under the will, says Clarke.

An equalisation payment may need to be made here too.

“Making a really well written caretaker’s agreement allowing the brother to go into the property now and taking the subsequent steps could potentially be the most tax-efficient thing for them to do,” says Clarke.

So, the brother would sell his own house and move into the father’s house. Qualifying for dwelling house relief will depend on his father living for three years.

After their father’s death, the siblings can do a deed of family arrangement, or the reader could distribute the estate assets in specie, appropriating the house to the brother, with equalisation payments, as necessary.

]]><![CDATA[US comedy gag about a sister who quits job to care for dad is no joke]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000

If you didn’t laugh, you may have cried – or maybe you did both – after watching Saturday Night Live’s Sister sketch when it flooded into family and friends’ messaging apps earlier this month.

In the American comedy programme’s skit, a son realises his ageing father needs more care at home but he doesn’t want to put Dad in a nursing home and live-in care could cost thousands.

He says: “I didn’t know where to turn. That’s when I heard about Sister. Sister is a live-in 24/7 eldercare provider that is completely free and also … your sister.

“Signing up couldn’t be easier. Simply text ‘Dad fell’ to Sister and she will quit her job, break her lease and move halfway across the country to take care of him.”

She manages medications, handles doctors, insurance companies and pharmacists, and can even bring her reluctant husband along – all without affecting the son’s 50 per cent share of the inheritance – because the parents’ will predates their dementia. Now, the son says, “I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”

The parody ends with “Quantities are limited. Sister may break down without warning. Offer void if Sister has a good therapist.”

The comedy lands so well because it’s painfully true. “When care intensifies, women’s employment pays the price,” according to the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE). When care is unavailable, unaffordable or does not meet families’ needs, someone has to fill the gap. Too often, that someone is a woman.

“What may begin as a private decision about how a family organises care can therefore have very broad consequences for employment, income and gender equality,” says EIGE.

Of course, plenty of men look after their parents and children, too. But as care responsibilities intensify over time, it’s women who are substantially more likely than men to leave employment. Lower-income carers, who tend to be women, are most exposed to care-related employment penalties. EIGE says “27 per cent of lower-income carers report reducing working hours or leaving employment due to care, compared with 20 per cent of middle-income carers and 17 per cent of higher-income carers”.

The big squeeze

With an estimated one in nine people in the workforce both caring for a loved one and managing their career, employers need to start future-proofing their employee benefits. The numbers are probably going only one way due to our ageing population but supports, both private and public, are limited.

In Ireland, employer-funded carer supports fall into two main categories: dedicated paid carer leave, which is still rare, and structured, carer-friendly workplace programmes. which are unpaid and more common in large employers.

The State offers limited supports for carers. Under the Carer’s Leave Act, eligible employees can take unpaid leave of between 13 and 104 weeks to provide full-time care to a qualifying person. Employees may qualify for Department of Social Protection payments such as carer’s benefit (PRSI-based) or carer’s allowance (means-tested). There’s also statutory medical care leave of up to five days of unpaid leave in a 12-month period.

Family Carers Ireland (FCI) estimates there are more than 624,000 family carers, and that at least 270,000 are balancing paid work with care. FCI thinks the number of working carers is even higher than that, as many people do not see themselves as carers. They see themselves simply as wives, daughter, sons or neighbours.

When South East Technological University surveyed its staff after joining FCI’s Caring Employers programme, 60 per cent identified as family carers. Most employers simply never ask this question, so the numbers are hard to quantify.

Ibec’s Better Care Better Business report, published in March 2024, gives us a snapshot of what this costs carers who also work outside the home. Of the carers surveyed, 63 per cent were in employment and 73 per cent of those found it challenging to balance work and care. Some 57 per cent reported added financial pressure and more than a third said caring had affected their careers.

Carers are often exhausted and don’t know where to turn for support. While 57 per cent said their employer had been flexible, only 29 per cent were aware of a company policy on caring and just 21 per cent had ever received paid leave for it. Most support seems to depend on company or managerial goodwill.

‘I care for my elderly parents, but my efforts are taken for granted. I think I might be going mad’

FCI’s State of Caring 2026 report, based on responses from 2,930 carers, describes the reality of informal unpaid supports. Some 71 per cent say caring has harmed their health, and the same proportion find it difficult to make ends meet.

When caring responsibilities become unmanageable, employees are often forced to make difficult choices. Some reduce their hours, others take extended leave and many leave the workforce altogether, often permanently. Carers who remain in work report less loneliness than those who have left, which is one reason the charity wants carers kept in employment wherever possible.

Amongst women: Why are there so few men in caring roles?

The cost to employers in recruitment, training and lost institutional knowledge is significant, and it is largely avoidable. Unaddressed caregiving interruptions carry real costs, including an estimated €615 million annually in Ireland from eldercare-related work disruptions alone, says FCI.

Small, practical actions can make a meaningful difference to employees such as offering flexible working options, showing understanding during challenging periods, encouraging open and respectful conversations, providing access to leave and wellbeing supports, communicating information on rights and entitlements through human resources and fostering empathetic leadership.

‘All the caring I put into my parents – the time, effort and money – is gone, wasted’

Employer toolkit

  1. Find out who your carers are. Run an anonymous survey. Most will not volunteer the information and many do not use the word carer.
  2. Write a carer policy and publicise it. If only three in 10 carers know a policy exists, it’s not doing its job.
  3. Train line managers. When flexibility is granted informally, it’s only as good as the next manager.
  4. Offer to pay for some carer days beyond the legal requirement, and ensure that dependents include parents, in-laws and other relatives. Family comes in many shapes and sizes.
  5. Make flexibility two-way. Offer workers compressed or reduced hours with an agreed route back to full hours when care needs change.
  6. Introduce a carer passport so arrangements do not have to be renegotiated after every restructure or new manager.
  7. Provide practical information. In the middle of a crisis, most people first need to understand home supports, the Fair Deal scheme and enduring power of attorney. The local HSE home support office or public health nurse is often the first port of call.
  8. Plan for the carers you will have. With an ageing population, employees who are not carers today will be tomorrow so explore those pathways now.

So, what’s the real cost of the Sister gag? The punchline is that Sister is free. She’s not. The cost shows up in her health, her hours, her reduced pension pot and her lost promotion prospects. Eventually it shows up for her employer too, in turnover and lost experience, when she decides the only way to manage is to leave.

Employers can’t make relatives share the load. But they can stop assuming that someone’s sister – who might also be their best employee – will absorb it.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

The net outcome has been weighed down by finance costs of high borrowings since the takeover by chairman Bob Etchingham, chief executive Joe Barrett and a unit of US private equity giant Blackstone.

Blackstone Infrastructure Partners owns 59.5 per cent of the group, which operates 440 locations across Ireland, the UK and US, including 200 large-scale motorway service areas and travel plazas.

The group employs about 18,000 people, and its outlets serve more than 180 million customers annually.

The group’s total borrowings amounted to €2.79 billion at the end of December, including €1.23 billion of bank loans, €281.3 million of high-cost junior debt, known as payment-in-kind notes, owed to Blackstone, almost €900 million of lease contracts, and other liabilities.

Gross finance costs rose to €188.7 million last year from €158.4 million in 2024. However, the group has remained highly profitable at earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) level since the deal.

Ebitda, one of the most important figures for the company’s finance providers, rose to €304 million last year from €296.9 million, even as revenues declined by 16 per cent to €3.24 billion, due to the disposal of its UK filling station business.

“Applegreen had another very satisfying performance in 2025,” Barrett said in a statement accompanying the publication of the results. “As we continue to redevelop our acquired sites, particularly in the US, and to grow organically, we expect our Ebitda to increase further in the coming years.”

Applegreen received €202.7 million in cash for the UK filling stations business, known as Petrogas Group UK and comprised of 98 locations, to UK rival EG On The Move. The deal delivered a capital gain of €121.2 million.

The sale did not affect Applegreen’s Welcome Break business in the UK, which also includes its operations in Northern Ireland. The UK remains the company’s largest market by revenues.

Applegreen has invested €750 million into its business over the past two years, as the group continued a significant expansion programme at home and abroad, the company said in a statement on Wednesday.

It had originally planned to invest €1 billion over the five-year period to 2029, but it has accelerated its investments in Ireland, the UK and the US to take advantage of significant opportunities in each of its three markets, including growing its electric vehicle-charging network in all three markets. It expects the investment spend to top €1 billion next year.

However, Applegreen walked away in September last year from a contentious 35-year deal to operate 18 motorway service areas in Massachusetts, amid legal threats from the underbidder for the contract. Massachusetts Department of Transport subsequently decided to launch a new procurement process earlier this year. Applegreen had planned to invest more than $750 million (€685 million) in the network.

]]>joe

   <title>Huthis rücken auf große Städte vor</title>
   <description>Millionen Menschen leiden im Krieg zwischen den proiranischen Huthis und  den von den Saudis gestützten Regierungstruppen. Am Donnerstag gab es laut Riad neue Raketenangriffe der Huthis. Die UNO und Hilfsorganisationen warnen vor einer humanitären Katastrophe. Militärisch sind die Huthis seit Wochen scheinbar unaufhaltsam auf Vormarsch. Die Großstadt Tais belagern die Huthis bereits, und sie rücken mittlerweile auf die provisorische Hauptstadt Aden vor. Unklar ist, ob die Regierungstruppen rechtzeitig ihre Differenzen beilegen.</description>

   <description>Im Ringen um ein neues EU-Budget hat es Donnerstagabend keinen Durchbruch gegeben. Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com regular summaries of news from Poland Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:59:56 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9 https://notesfrompoland.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/cropped-2019-10-29_1838-32x32.png Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com 32 32 Court overturns Warsaw mayor’s ban on protest outside Constitutional Tribunal https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/27/court-overturns-warsaw-mayors-ban-on-protest-outside-constitutional-tribunal/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:59:54 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107572

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

A court has overturned the mayor of Warsaw’s decision to ban the ongoing demonstration taking place outside the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in protest against the takeover of the TK by a group of government-backed judges.

While the mayor, who is a deputy leader of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, argued that the gathering threatened public safety, Warsaw’s district court found that banning it completely was too “radical” a step.

Sąd uchylił decyzję stołecznego ratusza odmawiającą przedłużenia zgody na zgromadzenie pod TK#PAPinformacje pic.twitter.com/kBLm9kT9vc

— Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) November 26, 2026

Protesters have been present in front of the TK since mid-September, fearing that the government would make a move to take control of the tribunal from its chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.

On 30 October, a group of eight judges appointed to the TK this year by Tusk’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – did indeed seize control of the tribunal and announced that Święczkowski had been suspended.

They avoided the demonstrators who were blocking the tribunal’s main gate by entering through a side entrance that leads in from the prime minister’s chancellery.

 

On Wednesday this week, city hall announced that mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had refused a request from the organiser of the protest for the public gathering in front of the TK to be allowed to continue from the end of November through to early January.

The municipal authorities said that the demonstration had blocked the busy road outside the tribunal, thereby hindering access for emergency vehicles. They also pointed to a number of “dangerous incidents”, including aggression towards the police by participants in the protest.

Such developments “have caused the gathering to lose its peaceful character”, wrote city hall. There are also “grounds to assume that the intention is, in effect, a long-term blockade of the entrance to the Constitutional Tribunal and the street itself”.

The mayor’s decision was condemned by the opposition, with PiS party leader Jarosław Kaczyński calling it “authoritarianism in its purest form” and a “trampling of citizens’ constitutional rights” to freedom of assembly and speech.

Warsaw's mayor, who is deputy leader of Poland's main ruling party, has refused permission for opposition protests outside the constitutional court to continue, saying they threaten public safety.

The opposition has condemned the "authoritarian" decision https://t.co/b6fIsqXzDH

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 25, 2026

The organisers of the gathering had the right to appeal the decision within 24 hours, which they exercised. And late on Thursday, Warsaw’s district court announced that it had overturned Trzaskowski’s prohibition of the gathering.

The information provided by city hall “does not provide grounds to assume that the assembly violates the rules for organising assemblies and may pose a threat to people’s life or health or to property to a significant extent”, found judge Anna Bonkowska-Kubek.

“The court holds the view that the most radical measures in the form of a ban on demonstrations can only be applied in very exceptional cases, and the authorities must always first consider actions and decisions that would enable the peaceful holding of the planned assembly,” she added.

A prohibition of a gathering “can only be applied in absolute exceptional circumstances, and the authorities must always first consider actions and decisions that would enable the peaceful holding of the planned assembly”, said the judge.

Bezprawna decyzja prezydenta Warszawy Rafała Trzaskowskiego zakazująca zgromadzenia przed Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym uchylona przez sąd!

Kolejni sędziowie nie chcą ochraniać nielegalnych decyzji polityków Koalicji Obywatelskiej, a tym samym żyrować ich swoim nazwiskiem.

To…

— Jarosław Kaczyński (@OficjalnyJK) November 26, 2026

The court’s ruling was welcomed by Kaczyński, who said that it showed how “judges are refusing to protect the illegal decisions of Civic Coalition politicians”. He called on supporters to join him for a further protest outside the TK at 3 p.m. on Sunday.

However, Bonkowska-Kubek’s decision was questioned by Tusk’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek. “I’m always a supporter of freedom of speech and the right to protest,” he told broadcaster RMF on Friday morning. “However, I would very much like the court to approach this rationally.”

Żurek said that, due to the effective blockade of the TK by the demonstrators, it is not possible for people to exercise their right to file cases to the tribunal in person.

Later on Friday morning, Trzaskowski announced that, while he “respects the court’s decision”, the city would exercise its right to issue a further appeal against Bonkowska-Kubek’s ruling.

Szanuję decyzję sądu, ale skorzystamy z prawa do zażalenia. Chodzi o mieszkańców i o służby ratunkowe, które muszą przejechać przez Aleję Szucha. Wolność zgromadzeń – tak. Blokowanie ulicy przez ponad miesiąc – nie.

— Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) November 27, 2026

The legal situation at the TK itself remains under dispute. The group of eight government-backed judges have begun holding meetings and processing cases, including stripping Święczkowski of legal immunity to face criminal charges.

However, Święczkowski and Nawrocki continue to insist that the actions of those judges are unlawful and that their decisions have no legal effect.

]]> Polish PM orders alternative financing channel for constitutional court after central bank freezes accounts https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/26/polish-pm-orders-alternative-financing-channel-for-constitutional-court-after-central-bank-freezes-accounts/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:29:25 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107536

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk has issued an order for the National Development Bank (BGK) to provide financing for the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after Poland’s central bank froze the TK’s accounts following a disputed takeover of the court by government-backed judges.

The relevant funds for the TK to function will be allocated by the finance ministry, announced government spokesman Adam Szłapka on Thursday morning, a day after the cabinet approved a resolution authorising the move.

However, the ousted chief justice of the court has condemned the government’s actions as “completely unlawful” and said that they make the court’s current leadership “directly subordinate” to the prime minister.

Premier @DonaldTusk wydał dyspozycję, by Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego zapewniał finansowanie Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, a środki na ten cel zabezpieczy minister finansów. Państwo musi działać.

— Adam Szłapka (@adamSzlapka) November 26, 2026

The move marks the latest twist in a long-running battle for control over the TK, which dates back around a decade to the unlawful appointment to the court of three judges under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.

As a result, Tusk’s centrist government, which took power from PiS in 2023, had effectively ignored the court and its rulings until this year, when it began appointing new judges to fill a growing number of vacancies on the TK’s 15-person bench.

Events came to a head on 30 October, when the eight judges appointed by Tusk’s majority in parliament – five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – seized control of the court.

They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under PiS, had been suspended. Święczkowski, backed by Nawrocki and PiS, rejected their actions as an illegal “coup d’état” and maintains he is the rightful head of the court.

 

The disputed status of the TK’s leadership led the National Bank of Poland (NBP) to announce earlier this month that it had frozen all outgoing transfers from TK accounts.

The central bank cited conflicting claims over who had the authority to manage the institution, saying it “has no authority to decide who is legally entitled to control the Constitutional Tribunal”.

The NBP is led by Adam Glapiński, who was appointed under PiS and is a longtime associate of party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Tusk’s government condemned the bank’s decision as politically motivated and pledged to find alternative ways of securing the tribunal’s finances.

Meanwhile, both Święczkowski and Anna Korwin-Piątkowska, the government-backed judge who has assumed leadership of the court, each appealed to Glapiński to unblock the Constitutional Tribunal’s accounts and recognise their respective authority to manage the court’s funds.

Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal, citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a takeover by a group of judges backed by the government https://t.co/ZYkzoneojO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 17, 2026

On Wednesday, the government adopted a resolution “on taking measures necessary to prevent a crisis situation related to the functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal” due to the NBP’s decision to freeze its accounts.

“At a time when, after many years, an opportunity has arisen to overcome the constitutional crisis, restricting the Constitutional Tribunal’s ability to exercise its constitutional powers will negatively affect the level of legal certainty for individuals, including citizens,” the resolution reads.

It requires the prime minister and finance minister to take “appropriate measures to protect the interests of the State Treasury and to ensure the state’s internal security and public order.”

Szłapka subsequently announced that Tusk had instructed BGK, a state-owned development bank, to provide financing to the tribunal.

The dispute around Poland's constitutional court risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/mtgutqSTQh

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026

Jan Grabiec, head of the prime minister’s chancellery, on Thursday morning told broadcaster TVN24 that the tribunal had an “auxiliary account” at BGK. This would allow its day-to-day operations to be financed despite the NBP’s decision to block payment orders, he added.

“It is not just a matter of ordinary tribunal staff potentially not receiving their salaries,” said Grabiec. “The State Treasury also bears responsibility for contracts entered into by the tribunal’s previous leadership that include specific payment deadlines.”

“This creates a liability for damages, potentially amounting to losses of many millions of zloty,” he added. “We cannot allow the State Treasury to be exposed to losses resulting from such politically motivated decisions of the National Bank of Poland.”

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

On Thursday, Święczkowski condemned the government’s decision to channel money to the TK through BGK, calling it “completely unlawful”, reports the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily.

“If this usurper Anna Korwin-Piotrowska accepts money from Tusk’s government, it will mean she is directly subordinate to Tusk,” he added.

At the time of writing, the NBP had not publicly commented on the government’s decision to channel funding to the tribunal through BGK. BGK, meanwhile, told PAP that it could not comment on the details of its arrangements with other parties, citing banking secrecy.
