]]> Warsaw hospital accused of offering “VIP access” for politicians fined 2.3 million zloty https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/26/warsaw-hospital-accused-of-offering-vip-access-for-politicians-fined-2-3-million-zloty/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:33:33 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107534

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The Warsaw hospital at the heart of a recent scandal over allegations that politically connected patients were given preferential treatment has been fined 2.3 million zloty (€520,000) after an investigation found that it admitted patients out of turn and doctors were absent during scheduled shifts.

The doctor at the centre of the scandal, who was a local councillor for Poland’s main ruling party, was charged with fraud in October and is now also facing disciplinary proceedings over alleged breaches of medical ethics and professional standards.

Niestety – Dawid K. jednak nie posiadł daru bilokacji, cudu nie było.

Z ustaleń kontrolerów Narodowego Funduszu Zdrowia wynika, że po prostu oszukiwał. Ale to nie jest tylko sprawa jednego młodego medyka z legitymacją Koalicji Obywatelskiej w torbie. Cały ten przypadek wiele… pic.twitter.com/DfC35LLUpo

— OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) November 26, 2026

The audit was conducted by the National Health Fund (NFZ), which finances public healthcare in Poland. It was carried out following a series of revelations in June by media outlets about alleged irregularities at the hospital.

Many of the claims centred around a young doctor, who can be identified only as Dawid K. under Polish privacy law due to the criminal proceedings against him. He served as coordinator of emergency services at the Southern Hospital.

News outlet Zero.pl was the first to report that the doctor, who also served as a local politician for the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that leads Poland’s ruling coalition, worked a seemingly impossible number of hours at four different hospitals and earned 1.6 million zloty last year alone.

The website alleged that the doctor had declared shifts when he was actually not present and cited instances in which he reportedly appeared in local media during hours when he was officially listed as being on duty at the hospital.

❗️ Błyskawiczne przyjęcia, wykonywanie pakietów kilkunastu, a nawet kilkudziesięciu badań w bardzo krótkim czasie, możliwość przebywania w innym pomieszczeniu niż ogół pacjentów. W Warszawskim Szpitalu Południowym stworzono nieoficjalnie szybszą i bardziej komfortową ścieżkę… pic.twitter.com/3aanpRVeBu

— Patryk Słowik (@PatrykSlowik) June 17, 2026

Over the following weeks, Zero.pl and two other news websites, Wirtualna Polska and Onet, revealed further alleged cases of huge salaries for some doctors and impropriety at the Southern Hospital, including preferential treatment for patients with political connections.

This included claims that there was a “VIP lounge” in which patients with connections to KO were given more comfortable facilities than others and that such patients were often allowed to skip the queue and receive treatment more quickly.

 

In its audit of the Southern Hospital, the NFZ found that certain patients had been admitted out of turn. Inspectors also identified cases in which patients in stable condition were admitted to the emergency department ahead of others whose health condition warranted more urgent attention.

The NFZ also found that doctors were absent during scheduled shifts and and that medical services were sometimes provided by staff without the required qualifications. The audit raised further concerns about the appointment of an inexperienced doctor as the coordinator of the emergency department.

In a statement published on Wednesday, the hospital acknowledged the NFZ’s fine but noted that it was a preliminary decision and that the hospital could submit objections. It said that its board was reviewing the details before deciding on its next steps.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

After announcing the end of its audit, the NFZ noted that it would forward the findings to prosecutors who have been investigating reports of irregularities at Southern Hospital.

Prosecutors last month charged Dawid K. with fraud, alleging that he submitted fraudulent or unreliable invoices to the hospital worth more than 583,000 zloty. He has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors are also investigating other cases of alleged wrongdoing at the hospital. However, a spokesman last month said that the findings so far do not confirm reports of a “VIP lounge” at the hospital.

Meanwhile, on Thursday, the spokesman for the National Chamber of Physicians (NIL), Poland’s medical professional body, announced that they had decided to bring disciplinary proceedings against Dawid K.

The claims against him concern alleged improper performance of medical duties, breaches of professional ethics, and conduct that undermined public trust in the medical profession.

Zgodnie z obietnicą przekazuję do wiadomości publicznej:

Rzecznik Odpowiedzialności Zawodowej podjął decyzję o przedstawieniu zarzutów Dawidowi K.

Dotyczą one rzetelności wykonywania zawodu, naruszenia etyki i podważenia zaufania do zawodu lekarza.

Będziemy informować o…

— Piotr Pisula (@PanPisula) November 26, 2026

In the wake of the allegations against him, Dawid K. resigned from his seat on the local council, left KO, and stopped working at the Southern Hospital. His former party also distanced itself from him.

Jan Grabiec, the prime minister’s chief of staff and head of the KO in the Mazovia province, which includes Warsaw, told reporters in June that the scandal “has no connection to KO, but since he was a KO councillor, we will be all the more stringent in holding those responsible to account”.

In July, the health minister, Jolanta Sobierańska-Grenda, unveiled a series of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in the healthcare system. They include caps on doctors’ salaries, a requirement for them to work at least half their statutory working time at a designated hospital, and a new electronic waiting list system.

Meanwhile, the mayor of Warsaw, Rafał Trzaskowski, who is also a deputy leader of KO, ordered a separate municipal audit of the hospital, which revealed a number of irregularities, including in relation to Dawid K.’s activities. It concluded with 44 recommendations that Trzaskowski said were being implemented.

]]> Poland plans no-fly zone on eastern border to aid downing of Russian missiles https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/25/poland-plans-no-fly-zone-on-eastern-border-to-aid-downing-of-russian-missiles/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:19:56 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107508

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland’s defence ministry has announced plans to establish a no-fly zone along the country’s eastern border with the aim of making it easier to shoot down Russian missiles and drones that violate Polish airspace.

Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has again suggested that Poland should be allowed to shoot down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards the Polish border. However, the defence ministry acknowledged today that NATO is so far opposed to the idea.

Wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk zapowiedział wprowadzenie strefy zakazu lotów przy wschodniej granicy Polski.

Jak poinformował minister Tomczyk, rozporządzenie trafiło do rządowego zespołu, strefa ma obejmować od kilkunastu do 50 kilometrów przy granicy wschodniej Polski i ma… pic.twitter.com/3xF68uNNRU

— Dariusz Wiewiorka (@darekwiewiorka) November 25, 2026

Speaking on Wednesday at the opening of a new military satellite imaging centre, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that his department “will request the government to establish a no-fly zone on the country’s eastern border, to ensure Poland’s security”.

Tomczyk acknowledged that, after three Russian missiles struck southeastearn Poland last Friday, NATO had offered support, including the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland.

“But at the same time, the Polish military must do everything possible to protect our interests here and now,” he added.

Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday.

Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment.

The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall.

“Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening.

“Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added.

The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express.

“The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper.

“We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added.

Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw

The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation.

 

The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking.

This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions.

The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope.

The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates.

Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector

The observatory also features a computer coordinating its measurements, a camera showing almost the entire sky, and a weather monitoring system. Observations will depend on atmospheric conditions and visibility.

“Examples of how this telescope might be used include photographing the cosmos and conducting simple research, such as measuring changes in the brightness of stars and producing graphs illustrating these changes,” explained Ewa Konarzewska from Gocław Culture Terminal.

Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector.

Last year, the country launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest-ever contract with the European Space Agency, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites.

Meanwhile, 2025 also saw astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski become the second-ever Pole to travel into space, as part of an ESA mission to the International Space Station.

The objects struck at three different locations in southeastern Poland – Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Mołodycz – not far from the Ukrainian border. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has taken some of its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident, leaving some benefit claimants unable to access their accounts.

The government confirmed on Friday morning that it had shut down some services as a precaution, with Universal Credit claimants reporting difficulties signing into their online accounts.

The department is working with GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate the incident and restore services.

Officials stressed that regular benefit and pension payments would not be affected by the disruption.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department said.

“We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.”

The government has yet to disclose the nature or scale of the incident, whether any personal data has been compromised or when it expects services to be fully restored.

DWP warns claimants over suspicious messages

The department, which is responsible for administering Britain’s welfare and state pension systems, urged those unable to access online services to try again later.

Universal Credit claimants typically use their online accounts to check payment dates, report changes in circumstances and communicate with their work coaches.

The DWP also reminded claimants to remain vigilant against potentially fraudulent messages.

“As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links,” it said.

The attack raises fresh questions over the resilience of Britain’s public sector digital infrastructure and the ability of government departments to maintain essential services during cyber disruption.

MPs have urged the government to accelerate its crackdown on so-called fake discounts to ensure it protects shoppers by Black Friday next year.

Parliament’s business select committee has called on Andy Burnham to stop shoppers from being “bombarded” with misleading promotions, as the body criticised Amazon and John Lewis for refusing to co-operate with its inquiry.

As Black Friday kicks off, shoppers will be hoping to take advantage of hefty discounts at a time when consumer confidence is near a 10-year low. But MPs have said they are worried Brits are being taken advantage of.

The committee’s report said: “British consumers are losing billions because misleading prices, online scams and unsafe products are not being adequately prevented or punished. These risks go up in the run-up to Black Friday.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to crack down on misleading discounts and subscription traps, as part of his pledge to provide households with “everyday fixes”, but these new rules are still being consulted on so have not arrived in time for this year’s Black Friday.

Liam Byrne, chair of the committee, said: “By Black Friday next year, we want fake discounts explicitly banned, tougher penalties for those who break the rules and proper protection for consumers, however they pay.

“Honest retailers deserve a level playing field and British shoppers should be able to hunt for a bargain without having to hunt for the truth.”

Misleading prices cost shoppers £10.6bn in the year May 2024, according to the National Centre for Social Research. Consumer group Which? has claimed that only a fifth of the discounts during Black Friday in 2025 offered the cheapest price that year.

The committee invited consumer giants John Lewis, Amazon and TIkTok to give evidence to its investigation but they all declined to appear and explain how they protect shoppers, it said.

Discount rules ‘unreasonable’

The MPs have called on the government to set up a consumer protection plan within six months, propped up by a named minister, multiple targets and measurable results.

Byrne added: “At a time when millions of families are counting every penny in the run-up to Christmas, British shoppers are being bombarded with fake discounts, false promises and fraudulent offers.”

Sue Davies, head of consumer protection policy at Which?, said: “Clearer rules on misleading pricing would reduce the legal hurdles regulators face and help create a level playing field for businesses that price honestly.”

Existing crackdowns on discounting have proved unpopular among some retailers, which claim that they pose an undue burden on companies and make it difficult for them to give shoppers value for money.

Chris Wootton, the finance chief of Frasers Group, which has had adverts banned over allegedly misleading discounts, said in September that the existing rules pose “unreasonable and we say unlawful barriers in the way of vigorous price competition in the market”.

Modern sport is obsessed with the future: innovation, disruption, new formats, new audiences. Yet paradoxically the things that often make sport matter are old-fashioned: records, rivalries, heroes and history.

It’s why starting a new sporting competition is such a difficult business. You can build it but – to paraphrase Field of Dreams – will they come? The last few weeks have shown the knife-edge of that gamble.

We’ve seen rugby’s inaugural Nations Championship and Uefa’s Nations League burst into life, while on the other side of the coin (and it’s a mighty big coin) LIV Golf has found a bunker it can’t escape from.

It got me thinking: it can’t just be luck, or funding. There must be some science to why some competitions succeed and others stutter. And increasingly that answer lies not in economics but in sociology. 

Before we start comparing apples with oranges, I should note that, of course, not all new competitions are the same.

You have creationary competitions that build something entirely new, often giving growing sports a competitive stage for the first time. Examples include the UFC, X Games and Premier Padel Tour. 

Then you have evolutionary competitions that take something familiar and give it a new environment. The Nations League and Nations Championship both fall into this category, so too the Laver Cup in tennis and football’s Club World Cup.  

Finally, you have revolutionary competitions. The IPL, Formula E, The Hundred, TGL, King’s League, LIV;  they are noisiest and most controversial but face the highest risk of failing. 

Despite these differences, they’re all trying to change fan behaviour. And their chance of success is not defined by money but meaning. 

Jeopardy, belonging, proof and lore

Meaning is everything in sport and it is an infuriatingly fragile thing for marketers to deal with. Hard to build and easy to break but, without it, new competitions don’t stand a chance.

The first challenge is jeopardy. For sport to mean anything, something needs to be on the line. Not just what you stand to win, but what you stand to lose. A trophy, a title, a place in the next round. 

LIV Golf’s organisers thought they were doing the right thing by creating the sport’s biggest financial prizes, but they failed to understand what any gambler will tell you: it’s also what you stand to lose that makes it matter. 

The second rule is belonging. People don’t just want to watch sport; they want to be part of it. This is what the IPL understood so brilliantly, giving cities their own teams and creating new loyalties. Similarly, the X Games gave a generation of action-sports fans a competition that reflected them and their culture. 

Belonging means a supporter is tying their fate to the supported. When they win the fan wins and vice versa. You can’t just invent that. It comes from a deeper social need, that a sporting team or individual becomes an extension of a fan’s own identity. 

The third principle is proof. Sport has meaning when that meaning is shared. Like money, it only has value if other people believe in it too. 

Sold-out stadiums and big broadcast deals help – one of the biggest coups for the Nations Championship was securing wall-to-wall coverage on ITV – but visibility is not the same as proof. 

Proof comes from how deeply people care. This is perhaps what King’s League and other influencer-led competitions struggle to understand. 

The final way to create meaning is through lore. By now we’re all familiar with the Drive To Survive effect, but while stories are powerful, legends are more so. 

Lore is not just about storytelling; it’s about history. Wales’s victory over New Zealand in the Nations Championship mattered because it was their first in a lifetime. 

This doesn’t mean new competitions can’t bring a freshness to sport, but if they can borrow from or tap into sporting lore then they are that much more likely to create the meaning that they need.

Most important facets are too often an afterthought

There they are; four rules to create meaning. Simple in theory, but perhaps less so in practice. And yet I suspect they’re often an afterthought when people set out to create a new sporting competition. 

The first conversation will usually be financial. How much do we need? Who’s going to invest? But if I was about to start a new competition, I would be focusing my energy more on meaning that money. 

Matt Readman is chief strategy officer at sports creative agency Dark Horses.

    There was a lot of coverage globally when Space X floated in June this year. Over 100,000 UK investors applied for shares (almost $1bn of orders) in what was the largest IPO in history. At the same time – others across the globe, including Germany, France, Japan, Australia and Canada were also investing. None of these countries had to re-write its rules to enable this as each of them used a gateway which was already established and set up. In the UK, this was the ‘Public Offer Platform Regime’ which the FCA brought into play this January. This effectively lets companies raising over £5m sell shares widely without a stock market listing.

    SpaceX was offering retail investors the opportunity to invest on the same terms as the big banks and institutions “pre-IPO”.  In many respects, the risk of the business mirror those of many private companies looking to scale up in the UK, just on a global scale. The time has come for a grown-up discussion about the benefits of investing in these types of companies as part of a diversified portfolio.

    Most of the growth of a company now happens before most of us get the opportunity to ‘buy in’. By the time everyday investors get their chance, much of the value has already gone to the funds and wealthy investors who were able to get in early. I think that if we want people to be able to share in the growth of the companies that they use every day then access before they list on the public markets matters as much as gaining access after an IPO.

    Of course, regulated crowdfunding (the UK being one of its pioneers) has been working to achieve this for more than a decade now yet the gateways that worked for Space X don’t work for (for example) a small fast-growing company in Manchester seeking investors from outside the UK. In the EU, there is one licence (ECSPR) which covers the whole single market yet even then only eight per cent of the money raised through EU crowdfunding platforms in 2024 came from investors outside of the platform’s own country.

    Mutual recognition

    What seems to be holding things back is a lack understanding and mutual recognition. Firms have strict limits on how much they can raise, compliance costs for platforms are huge, disclosures can’t easily be compared between countries and settlements are slow (and manual) for smaller issuers. But importantly each jurisdiction writes its rules in isolation treating the world outside the national boundary as almost irrelevant.

    Research from the Global Equity Crowdfunding Alliance (GECA) suggests that the fixes to these should be achievable by the policymakers, regulators and platforms that are in place now. Examples include recognising where national rules already achieve the same outcome across territories, secondary markets (allowing for an exit strategy) should be built at the same time as fundraising, a common baseline for what information investors are given could be agreed and new settlement technologies could be properly tested with findings both good and bad being published and shared.

    GECA has just released a position paper as a result of a global discussion about the Space X raise and its possible implications for the crowdfunding industry. The problems and suggested fixes that I mention above are included in the recommendations of that paper.

    I think that the UK is one of the territories that is in prime position to become the global hub for private market fundraising. Here in the UK, we have a regulator that has shown it can open new routes to market, a well-established and experienced crowdfunding industry and, when considering the Space X raise, we also have proof that British retail investors will turn up in their tens of thousands when they’re given a way in. I guess at the minute what is missing is the ambition to have it all joined up across borders. But that’s where GECA steps in.

    When I was a Treasury minister, I was struck by how crucial just three concepts are to the maths that every adult in the UK must understand: inflation, compound interest and spreading risk. These core principles underpin the vast majority of the big financial decisions adults will make in their lives, from taking out a mortgage, deciding which credit card offers the best value or investing in an ISA. And most immediate of all, the huge commitment to student debt – a 40-year obligation where the interest will compound relentlessly if they do not become high earners.

    It is therefore encouraging that the government has announced every child will be taught the ‘big three’, chiming with the Numeracy for Life Committee’s new report, Making it Count. In it, we identified these concepts as a benchmark for financial capability, and ministers deserve credit for putting them at the heart of what children will learn.

    I would now encourage them to go further and build on the momentum that’s already been generated. The report shows how much further as a society we need to go to put numeracy on an equal footing with literacy. Can you imagine the reaction if it was revealed 8m adults had the literacy skills of a nine-year-old? It would rightly generate immediate action; yet the fact the same number share the numeracy skills of a year four pupil does not. 

    Numeracy and the workforce

    Over recent months, my Committee heard from employers ranging from Santander and Barclays to National Grid, EDF and BT. Many said numeracy was a problem that needed attention, and many are running their own catch-up training programmes to get their employees up to speed. 

    But the industries of tomorrow will make us even more reliant on having a workforce that’s confident in its numbers. Employers told us that artificial intelligence in particular is increasing the need for better numeracy. 

    Central to this is a shift from calculation to judgement. That is, knowing whether the answer a chatbot produces actually makes sense. From financial services to energy and the digital economy, the sectors that will power Britain’s growth will depend on the workforce of tomorrow having the right judgement.

    So ministers should treat this announcement as a first step. Two more would make a real difference.

    What else is needed

    First, the teachers delivering these lessons are often not maths specialists. They need proper training in the concepts themselves, not just a new set of lesson plans. We all know the positive impact an engaging teacher can have. 

    Second, the red tape that makes it harder for employers to get into classrooms should be cut. The businesses we heard from are eager to show pupils why numbers matter, and we should let them. Too often pupils can’t see how the maths they learn in the classroom connects to the world of work. Seeing it applied would be transformational.

    The government is clearly listening and I commend them for it. However, if we are to tackle the systemic societal issues caused by poor numeracy it must now go further. I will be the first to praise them if they do.

A decision driven by the desire to save rather than a vision of what London’s civic heart should look like.     I want to see the next Mayor be passionate about the built environment and give London its mojo back. I’m calling for nothing short of an urban renaissance.

    In an interview with City AM, Harris said: “Some of this stuff needs to be done. But I do think it has led to pretty seismic changes in terms of how we think about pensions in the UK.

    “Every week there’s another piece of news out there on pension schemes you don’t necessarily expect.”

    She noted that while asset managers like Schroders are able to manage the wave of change through public policy teams, for the actual providers it can be hard to manage the workload, particularly as both the government and City watchdog are introducing various policies and consultations.

    “Trying to keep up with all the different policy frameworks that are being issued by all the various different regulators…not necessarily so much for us sitting in asset management, but if you think about the actual providers and how overwhelming it is for them, I think it can be really difficult,” she said.

    Large managers and master trusts boast sizable internal policy teams to manage the workload coming off the back of policy shakeups, but smaller single-employer trusts face a more difficult challenge in managing changes, Harris warned.

    In particular, the Value for Money framework, which is set to be implemented from 2028, has faced backlash for placing a greater burden on smaller schemes. 

    Master trusts spread fixed governance and reporting costs across thousands of members, but smaller schemes must compile the same annual datasets across a much smaller base, driving up costs and pushing more towards consolidation.

    The plans, dubbed ‘Guided Retirement’, will “resurrect” the option of having an inflation protected pension that provides a secure income for private sector retirees and prevents them from having to make complex financial decisions. 

    Harris, who was appointed head of UK Institutional in March of this year, noted that private sector providers “haven’t had to do [this] up until now”, but the growing number of defined contribution savers and retirees has forced the issue onto the government agenda.

    Changes to the law mean companies – including football clubs – can now be held liable for offences such as child abuse by their senior management and owners, write lawyers Helen Harvey and Charlotte Moss.

    Earlier this month, the Football Association launched Voices of Truth, a digital platform paying tribute to survivors of child sexual abuse in football.

    It marked 10 years since revelations by former footballers led the FA to commission an independent inquiry into historic abuse, which culminated in the Sheldon Review in 2021. But the anniversary is not just a moment to remember; it brings renewed attention on where accountability for misconduct in football should lie today.

    A recent change in the law raises an important question: could clubs themselves be prosecuted for alleged abuse by individuals? Since June, under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, companies can be held criminally liable for offences committed by senior managers while acting in the course of their role.  

    A senior manager is someone who plays a significant role in making decisions about, or managing, the whole or a substantial part of a company’s activities. But determining who counts as a senior manager is not straightforward.

    Prosecutors will look beyond an individual’s job title, employment status or pay to consider their influence over how the business is run. Government guidance makes clear that directors and senior officers, such as CFOs and COOs, would normally fall within the definition. Club owners may too, depending on how involved they are in its running. 

    However, senior management is not limited to board members or those performing executive roles, and could include those with significant responsibility for functions such as HR.

    For football clubs, this could extend to individuals not traditionally considered senior management. For example, coaches or those responsible for player selection, managing player contracts or overseeing a club’s grassroots programme could be caught, depending on their responsibilities. 

    Clubs may need to review safeguarding measures

    Crucially, the offence must have been committed while the senior manager was acting within the “actual or apparent scope of their authority”. This does not mean that the criminal conduct was authorised in some way – it just means it happened when the person was doing their job. 

    For instance, a coach who sexually assaults a player while demonstrating a technique during a training drill may be considered to be acting within the scope of their authority as the conduct occurred in the course of their coaching duties. The same could apply to a club CEO who uses a meeting about a player’s contract or future at the club to commit a sexual offence. 

    However, with no case law to consider, it is not yet clear who will qualify as a senior manager and when their conduct will fall within the scope of their authority. 

    The Act also makes it a criminal offence to deliberately prevent or discourage someone from reporting suspected child sexual abuse where they are legally required to do so. Although this “obstruction offence” has not yet come into force, once implemented, it could give rise to corporate liability if committed by a senior manager acting within the scope of their authority.

    Where allegations of criminal misconduct arise, football clubs must now consider their own potential corporate exposure, rather than dealing with the matter solely through internal disciplinary proceedings and individual accountability.

    Clubs may therefore want to revisit their training and safeguarding procedures to ensure they are robust and that the responsibilities of those in senior positions, including coaching staff, are clearly understood. 

    A decade on from survivors’ bravery in disclosing their experiences, the onus is now well and truly on clubs to do everything in their power to stamp out abuse.

    The argument for growth is beyond compelling, but not enough people understand why, writes John O’Brien

    Ask almost anyone what Britain needs most and the answer will be growth. But ask them why, and the conversation becomes more interesting. We seem to have become good at discussing how to grow our economy, yet less confident in discussing the kind of country we are trying to grow. To me, this is the key question.

    Of course we need economic growth; we need greater productivity, investment, innovation and enterprise, because without them, we cannot sustain our public services, defend ourselves against increasing external and internal threats and create opportunities for people or improve living standards. The argument for growth is therefore beyond compelling; it is the oxygen we need as a nation, but growth should surely be seen as more than simply an economic measurement, it should be an ambition for the country we want to become, the type of place we want for our children.

    The need for joined-up thinking

    After more than four decades in international businesses, in civil society and as a philanthropist, I know that our greatest challenge is not a shortage of ideas, talent or ambition. Our national issue is our inability to connect them sufficiently across the boundaries of sectors, the established thinking of 20th century institutions and the comfortable attitudes of some in maintaining the status quo. This combined fug, of trying to break down silos, avoid the doomsayers and find gaps between stifling regulations, so often holds us back from making things happen, but it also stifles our connected thinking.

    Consider the need for investing in a healthier population, in order to have a more productive workforce, which leads to reduced demands on our health services. Consider how better education can drive innovation and in turn build opportunities in the potential of more thriving towns and cities, in order that they will attract external investment and grow our national confidence. These individual aspects of our society should not be competing ambitions, they should be seen as mutually reinforcing foundations of prosperity and the reasoning behind growth in all these dimensions should shape the quality of life for us and the next generation.

    This is where I think there is an important question here for the City and for those responsible for investing in Britain’s capital. We are rightly sophisticated in measuring financial returns, managing risk and allocating investment but are we equally adept in recognising the wider conditions that create economic value over time?

    Growth benefits all sectors

    Businesses calculate the return on a new factory or the creation of a new technology platform, yet how often do we account for the economic returns from such things as better community health, stronger education results, well-functioning infrastructure or thriving communities? These should not simply be desirable social outcomes to be funded once growth has occurred, they are investments in the productive capacity of our people and our country. These factors should help shape where businesses can best flourish, where people thrive and where capital can earn a lasting return.

    None of what I describe here should mean abandoning financial discipline or pretending that every worthwhile initiative delivers the same return, rather it means taking a fuller view of what makes Britain attractive for long-term investment and recognising that government, business, investors and civil society each have a part to play in creating those conditions. However, too many people persist in discussing these things separately, through narrow perspectives of individual sectors, industries or political priorities. 

    There is another challenge, too, which is we have become very good at talking Britain down and whilst our difficulties are undoubtedly real, so too are our extraordinary strengths. I travel across the country and so I know there are people building remarkable businesses, developing groundbreaking technologies and strengthening their communities, but the truth is some of this happens despite wider government policy and not because of it. Perhaps, therefore we need to spend rather more time connecting the energy such individuals show, rather than hearing more about what is not working.

    The ‘UK Davos’

    This thinking is what led me to establish Anthropy, now the UK’s largest national leadership gathering, which has been nicknamed the “UK Davos”, but don’t blame me for that. It brings together leaders from all sectors at the Eden Project in Cornwall each March and what began as an experiment in national collaboration is now a gathering of 2,500 leaders, united not by political allegiance or profession, but by a shared determination to inspire a better Britain. For March 2027, we have chosen growth as our overarching theme but rather than simply focusing on GDP, we are asking four broader questions of growth in all its dimensions: How do we grow human flourishing? How do we grow vibrant places? How do we grow good prosperity? And how do we grow Britain’s global influence? 

    Together is how we grow a nation and together these questions will inform a National Growthprint, with the intention of presenting practical proposals for a Westminster launch next summer. This is not an argument for replacing economic growth with worthy aspirations, quite the opposite: it is recognition that lasting prosperity depends upon the strength of the economy which in turn is based on its people, places, institutions and relationships.

    Britain has no shortage of people talking about its future, but what we need are more people prepared to step forward to help shape it. That is why, next March, we will gather again at the Eden Project, not simply to discuss Britain’s challenges, but to explore what we might achieve together, because the most important question is not simply how much Britain can grow, but what kind of Britain that growth will create. 

    John O’Brien MBE is founder and chairman of Anthropy. Anthropy27 takes place at the Eden Project, Cornwall, 10th to 12th March 2027

    But the 12-member committee – which includes Bank governor Andrew Bailey and Financial Conduct Authority boss Nikhil Rathi – cautioned the funding behind AI was becoming increasingly “complex, circular and opaque”.

    The committee pointed to “more complex financial structures” as driving the interconnected risk. It said financing was spanning equity markets, public bond markets and private credit as well as less transparent measures.

    AI-related companies were providing finance to others in the sector, the FPC said, which was “strengthening sectoral interconnections”.

    The committee also raised the alarm on the development of quantum technology and called for the industry to “accelerate long-term preparations”.

    “They will also need credible arrangements to recover quickly from operational disruption, in order to maintain the provision of vital financial services. Taken together, these will place competing demands on technology skills and management capacity,” the FPC said.

We will continue to use our powers independently and robustly to protect consumers, support innovation, and drive growth.”

    Migration levels dropped to 77,000 in the year to June 2026, estimates by the Office for National Statistics showed.

    Total immigration of non-EU nationals in the 12-month period was 550,000, compared to 79,000 for EU nationals and 109,000 for Britons arriving. 

    Emigration levels of about 661,000 helped bring the net migration figure down significantly. In the previous 12-month period, net migration was at 204,000.

    The figures will likely relieve Labour government figures as immigration concerns have been pushed down the list of the British public’s voting priorities in recent months.

    But official data showed that about 19 per cent of total emigration came from British nationals aged between 16 and 34 leaving the country.

    Perfume suppliers to FTSE 100 giant Unilever have been fined more than €500m for running a “beer and curry” cartel in which bosses colluded to fix prices.

    The UK’s competition watchdog said three of the world’s biggest perfume makers, who have admitted to breaking the law, collaborated in WhatsApp groups and in person to keep prices high.

    Bosses at the Swiss and American perfumers shared sensitive information about their dealings with Unilever, one of the world’s biggest consumer products groups and the owner of brands like Domestos, Dove and Cif.

    The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said the perfume executives used these covert meetings and group chats to collectively refuse Unilever’s requests for them to lower prices. 

    The regulator said the suppliers used “WhatsApp messages, telephone calls and other communications” to discuss “how to respond to commercial negotiations, rather than deciding their approaches independently”.

    The watchdog added that some of these conversations took place at in-person “beer and curry” meetings in London. The years-long investigation into the perfume companies included raids on their offices in March 2023.

    The CMA fined the three manufacturers, Firmenich, Givaudan and International Flavors & Fragrances (IFF), £85m. This is in addition to the €471.9m in penalties imposed by the European Union’s (EU) competition watchdog, bringing the total fines to more than €500m.

    Cartels ‘can push up prices’

    Juliette Enser, the CMA’s executive director of competition enforcement, said: “Suppliers must set their prices and commercial strategies independently of each other. Exchanging sensitive information with competitors can weaken competition and leave business customers facing costs.

    “These were major international suppliers discussing information that should have remained confidential. Today’s fines should be a clear warning for all businesses: competitors must compete, not coordinate behind closed doors.”

    The perfume makers’ actions warned that cartel activity can also “ultimately feed through to higher prices” for customers. 

    The fines imposed on all three companies were discounted after they co-operated with the UK and EU investigations and settled with the authorities.

    Christian Stammkoetter, chief executive of Givaudan, said the behaviour regulators identified was “unacceptable”.

    An IFF spokesman said that the company “has accepted responsibility for improper conduct involving certain individuals, none of whom remain with the company”.

    DSM-Firmenich said its settlement was not an admission of liability. Their spokesperson added it had “cooperated fully” with investigators and said the settlement represented “the company’s commitment to maintaining the highest standards of compliance and business conduct”.

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That changed with the 2025 financial year. A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. What has held up is the type of company being funded: deep technology, rather than consumer apps or fintech, took 63 percent of all startup investment in 2024, led by rounds for the delivery-robot company Starship Technologies and the green-hydrogen firm Stargate Hydrogen.

What the density figure doesn’t tell you

A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

Other country-specific spin-offs followed the same pattern for a few years, each with its own name and its own small user base, before the company folded them together under a single brand, Vinted, as the parent business decided a fragmented set of local sites made less sense than one platform users could recognise anywhere in Europe. The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Vinted makes its money almost entirely from the buyer’s side of the transaction: a fixed fee of roughly $0.70 plus a variable fee of about 5 percent of the item’s price, charged in the buyer’s local currency (figures as of late 2025) — according to Vinted’s own Buyer Protection fee page. That fee funds Vinted’s Buyer Protection service, including secure payment handling and dispute support. Shipping is a separate charge paid by the buyer at checkout, even though the seller receives a prepaid label.
